The core mechanism here is Flying Blue's Promo Rewards program, and once you understand how it works, you'll never look at transatlantic business class the same way again.

Flying Blue is Air France-KLM's frequent flyer program and a member of the SkyTeam alliance. Unlike many loyalty programs that use a static award chart, Flying Blue uses dynamic pricing — meaning award costs fluctuate based on demand, route, and season. That sounds like a disadvantage, and for standard awards it often is. But Flying Blue offsets this with a monthly release of Promo Rewards: a curated list of routes where award seats are released at 25–50% below standard dynamic pricing, often with surcharges waived entirely.

Sources indicate that this is the inefficiency. When Air France wants to stimulate demand on a specific route in a given month, it uses Promo Rewards to attract award bookings. The airline gets seats filled; you get business class to Paris for 53,000 miles instead of potentially 80,000+ at standard dynamic rates. It's a win-win — if you know to look for it.

According to recent reports, the transfer ecosystem is what makes this accessible. Flying Blue partners with every major transferable points currency at a 1:1 ratio:.

The practical implication: if you hold a Chase Sapphire Preferred, Chase Sapphire Reserve, Amex Platinum, Amex Gold, Citi Strata Premier, Capital One Venture X, or Bilt Mastercard, you already have a direct pipeline to Flying Blue miles. Most transfers are instant, meaning you can spot a Promo Reward, confirm the seat exists, transfer points, and book — all in the same afternoon. That speed matters because Promo Reward seats can disappear quickly.

Industry observers note that one nuance worth naming: fuel surcharges. On standard Flying Blue awards for Air France and KLM-operated flights, the program passes through carrier-imposed surcharges that can add $200–$500 to your redemption. However — and this is critical — Promo Reward bookings typically eliminate these surcharges, meaning you pay the miles cost plus only government taxes. Always confirm surcharge status before booking a non-Promo award.

Sources indicate that finally, understand the routing rules: Flying Blue allows open-jaw itineraries, meaning you can fly into Paris and home from Amsterdam (or vice versa), effectively building a multi-city European trip with a single award booking. The booking window opens 359 days in advance — strategy accordingly.

According to recent reports, head to FlyingBlue.com at the beginning of each month — Promo Rewards are typically released in the first week. Navigate to the "Promo Rewards" section under the Awards tab. You're looking for transatlantic routes in business class (referred to as "Business" or "La Première" on the site). Bookmark the page and set a calendar reminder. You can also follow ChooseFI community forums, frequent flyer blogs, and Flying Blue's social accounts, which announce Promo Rewards as they drop. When a JFK–CDG or similar North America–Europe business class Promo Reward appears at 53,000 miles, you're in the window.

Once you've identified a Promo Reward route, search for availability directly on FlyingBlue.com. Use the award search tool, select "Business" class, and enter your travel dates. Promo Reward seats are labeled distinctly in the results. If you see them, note the exact flight numbers, dates, and total miles required before doing anything else. Don't transfer points yet — just confirm the seats exist and are bookable.

According to recent reports, initiate the transfer from your credit card rewards portal. Enter your Flying Blue membership number exactly as it appears on your account. For Chase and Amex, transfers post instantly — refresh your Flying Blue account and the miles should appear within minutes. For Capital One or Bilt, allow 1–2 days. For Marriott Bonvoy®, note the 3:1 ratio (you'll need 159,000 Bonvoy points for 53,000 Flying Blue miles) and allow 1–5 days.

It has been revealed that if Promo Reward seats aren't available on your dates, don't give up. Check standard award availability on Flying Blue — the pricing will be higher, but the experience is identical. Alternatively, set up alerts through third-party tools and revisit the search as your travel dates approach. Availability often opens closer to departure as airlines release unsold inventory.

Unlike most airline award programs that set a fixed or dynamic price and leave it, Flying Blue runs a monthly promotional cycle. At the beginning of each month, they release a list of routes with discounted award pricing. These Promo Rewards typically offer 25-40% off the standard mileage price and apply to both economy and business class. The discounted routes change every month, covering different destinations on a rotating basis. This means a route that is not on promotion this month may appear next month. The system rewards patience and monitoring: travelers who check the Promo Rewards page monthly and maintain transfer-ready points in Chase, Amex, or other programs can consistently find premium cabin deals to European destinations.

Let's walk through a real-world example that illustrates exactly why the ChooseFI community gets excited about this redemption.

The Booking: You're flying JFK → CDG in Air France Business Class on a Boeing 777-300ER. It's a Tuesday evening departure — one of the best days for award availability — and you've snagged a Promo Reward seat at 53,000 Flying Blue miles plus approximately $65 in government taxes.

The Cash Alternative: A quick search on Google Flights shows the same seat retailing for $4,200 on that date. That's not an anomaly — transatlantic business class averages $3,000–$6,000 depending on season and advance purchase. At $4,200 in cash versus 53,000 miles, you're extracting 7.9 cents per point in value. Your Chase Ultimate Rewards points just became extraordinarily potent.

It has been revealed that the Experience: You arrive at JFK and head to the Air France lounge before departure — accessible as a business class passenger. From the moment you board, the difference from economy is visceral. Your seat in the 1-2-1 configuration means no climbing over a stranger; you have direct aisle access. The seat fully reclines into a 180-degree flat bed with a thick mattress pad and proper bedding — not a glorified recliner, an actual bed. The meal service begins shortly after departure: a starter, a main course with real silverware, a cheese course, dessert, and a selection of French wines that would be at home in a Parisian bistro.

Seven hours later, you land at CDG having slept properly, eaten well, and arrived ready to explore Paris instead of recovering from an overnight in a middle seat. You step off the plane into Terminal 2E, collect your bags, and you're in the city within an hour.

The FI Math: Those 53,000 points came from everyday spending on your Chase Sapphire Reserve — grocery runs, gas, a few restaurant meals over the course of six months. You didn't buy the points. You earned them on purchases you were already making, transferred them in minutes, and unlocked a $4,200 experience for $65 out of pocket. That's the ChooseFI travel rewards system working exactly as designed.

Do this: Set a recurring monthly calendar reminder for Promo Rewards. Promo Rewards drop in the first week of each month and popular routes sell out fast. The readers who consistently land these redemptions aren't lucky — they're systematic. Mark the first Monday of every month as your "check Flying Blue" day.

Do this: Use an open-jaw routing to maximize your Europe trip. Flying Blue allows open-jaw itineraries, meaning you can fly into one city and out of another within a single award booking. Fly JFK → CDG, travel through France, and fly home from AMS → JFK. You've just built a multi-city trip without paying for positioning flights — and used a single 53,000-mile award to do it.

Industry observers note that do this: Transfer points only after confirming availability. This cannot be overstated. Transfers from Chase and Amex are instant, but they are also irreversible. Never initiate a transfer until you have confirmed, with your own eyes, that the award seat is available and bookable. The five-minute shortcut of transferring first has stranded miles in countless accounts.

Avoid this: Booking standard dynamic awards without checking Promo Rewards first. Flying Blue's dynamic pricing on standard awards can be significantly higher than Promo Reward pricing — sometimes 30–50% more miles for the exact same seat. Always check if the month's Promo Rewards include your route before defaulting to a standard award.

Industry observers note that avoid this: Ignoring the surcharge line item. On standard (non-Promo) Flying Blue awards for Air France flights, carrier surcharges can add $200–$500 to your out-of-pocket cost. This doesn't eliminate the value, but it changes the math. Always review the full fee breakdown before confirming. Promo Rewards typically waive these surcharges — another reason to prioritize them.

Do this: Stack earning across multiple cards. You don't need to earn 53,000 points on a single card. Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Membership Rewards, and Citi ThankYou Points all transfer to Flying Blue at 1:1. Accumulate across programs, then choose the best transfer source when a Promo Reward surfaces. This flexibility is a structural advantage of the ChooseFI approach to travel rewards.

Know your expiry window. Flying Blue miles expire after 24 months of account inactivity. Keep your account active with at least one transaction (even a small earning or redemption) every two years to protect your balance.

This redemption is built for the intentional traveler — someone who has spent time accumulating points on one or more major transferable currencies and is ready to deploy them strategically rather than cash them in for coffee and Amazon gift cards.

Minimum requirements: You'll want at least 53,000 points in a single transferable currency (Chase, Amex, Citi, Capital One, or Bilt) or the ability to combine balances to reach that threshold. No Flying Blue status is required — this is available to any member.

In a recent development, major US-to-Europe routes like JFK-CDG or JFK-AMS tend to appear on the Promo Rewards list every 2-4 months. Less popular routes may appear less frequently. The key is consistent monthly monitoring so you catch the promotion when it appears for your target destination.

According to recent reports, flying Blue does not offer formal stopover benefits on award tickets. However, you can book a one-way promo award to your gateway city and then add a separate low-cost carrier or train connection to your final destination. Many travelers use this strategy to explore Paris or Amsterdam for a few days before continuing onward.

Yes. Flying Blue miles expire after 24 months of account inactivity. Any qualifying activity resets the clock, including earning miles through a flight, credit card transaction, or transfer partner. A single small transfer from Chase or Amex every two years is sufficient to keep your miles alive.

Both airlines offer lie-flat business class seats with direct aisle access on long-haul aircraft. Air France's cabin tends to emphasize French culinary presentation and wine service, while KLM has a more understated Dutch design aesthetic. Both are solid products. When booking through Flying Blue, you can choose either airline based on routing, schedule, or cabin preference.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

It has been revealed that flying Blue Promo Rewards turn business class to Europe from a special-occasion splurge into a repeatable system. By monitoring monthly promotions, maintaining transfer-ready points across multiple programs, and booking when your route appears at a discount, you can consistently fly lie-flat to European destinations for 50,000-62,000 miles. The fuel surcharges are a real cost to factor in, but even with that overhead, promo business class awards deliver 5-12 cents per mile in value. Set the monthly reminder and let the system work.

Industry News: How Triathlon and Incurable Cancer Have Given Me a Way to Live Despite My Diagnosis

💡 Key Takeaways

  • I have always believed that if I worked hard enough and planned carefully enough, I might chart the course of my life.
  • Running and occasional triathlons are at the top of my goal-making lists.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: FinisherPix Powered by Outside).

Age-group triathlete Rebecca Jaussi shares her personal story with Triathlete of how receiving a cancer diagnosis drove her to signing up for and racing an Ironman 70.3.

I have spent most of my life making plans.

Endless lists of goals. Race calendars. Career milestones. Bucket-list adventures. I have always believed that if I worked hard enough and planned carefully enough, I might chart the course of my life.

Running and occasional triathlons are at the top of my goal-making lists.

In a recent development, I was a late starter professionally, choosing to stay home with my children when they were young. When I eventually returned to school, I didn’t ease my way back in. I was accepted into an accelerated doctoral nursing program, completing an intense year of coursework and clinicals before becoming a registered nurse, followed by three years of doctoral study. In 2020, I earned my doctorate in nursing practice and became a family nurse practitioner.

I have always been willing to push myself, physically and mentally, and my tenacity has benefited me.

I never imagined I would need it to fight cancer.

According to recent reports, this story began with a fall. It was another beautiful morning on the North Shore of Oahu (where I was living at the time) in February 2023, and I was running a technical trail when I went down on a rocky section. I experienced a pop in my right hamstring and some pain. But I did what I always do and just kept going.

I finished the run. I experienced some pain afterward, but not enough, in my mind, to stop running for good. I took a few days off and then returned to the trails.

As a healthcare provider, I knew better. But as a runner, I convinced myself otherwise.

It has been revealed that I continued running through an increasingly persistent, insidious pain. Eventually, my pace deteriorated from slow to a limping shuffle. Finally, I went to my colleague who practiced sports medicine, and was referred to physical therapy.

I started PT in May. My physical therapist told me I needed to stop running, and I thought that was an unreasonable course of action. There have been very few occasions in my life when I stopped running, including childbirth and surgery, and they were brief periods of time.

Running wasn’t simply exercise for me; it was where I found my flow state and truly part of my identity.

I didn’t feel ready or willing to give up running due to the pain but trusted my physical therapist, whom I considered a friend and a respected colleague, that this was the best course of action.

For three months, I walked on flat trails. I continued my physical therapy exercises and cross-trained but abstained from running or hiking.

When I returned for another assessment, my physical therapist was puzzled. I wasn’t improving. He suggested imaging, and that push changed everything.

According to recent reports, I went in for an MRI of my right leg. The imaging was ordered for my mid-thigh, which was not where I had originally injured my hamstring. When I discussed this with the technician, I pointed out that it was in my hip region, so he modified the imaging order.

The MRI indicated enlarged lymph nodes in my right groin, hip, and possibly behind my knee, which was an abnormal finding.

In a recent development, I had no recent infection or other obvious explanation for the swollen lymph nodes. I asked colleagues and peers for their opinions, and most believed this was a benign finding.

In a recent development, my mind vacillated between thinking that it was probably fine and the worst-case scenario of malignancy. It felt unsettling to me, and I decided to push for a biopsy rather than wait a few months for an ultrasound to see if the lymph nodes were still enlarged.

After the biopsy, I waited eight grueling days for the results. The physician, who was also my colleague and friend, told me the findings indicated that I had a form of B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

Industry observers note that this was not easy to ingest, but I didn’t want to burden her with the heaviness of this diagnosis and began joking around. I was blasé and asked her, “How are we going to fix my leg so that I can run?” refusing to fall apart on the phone.

Then I hung up and broke down in front of my husband. Suddenly, all the aims I had spent my life making seemed irrelevant. Questions revolved in my head. What would happen to my family? My future? My career?

The next step I took was to do what I knew how to do, which was research my diagnosis to find out everything that I could about it. I wanted to know the prognosis, treatment options, statistics, anything to help me wrap my head around this.

What I discovered in this process was much more difficult to accept. There were things that I could not control.

According to recent reports, I was driven to face the possibility that I may not live as long as I had expected. I had to accept that I would be living with the uncertainty of my health status and that fighting incurable cancer might become a permanent fixture in my life.

For someone who had devoted decades to building goals and marking off boxes, this was terrifying. There were no checklists for this.

I took time to process what I was facing and came to the recognition that I had a choice – not about living with cancer, but about living my life.

Most importantly, I still wanted to run.

I was not going to allow this diagnosis to define me; I had a strong desire to live my life to the fullest with purpose and direction. I still wanted to work as a nurse practitioner for as long as I could. I still wanted to pursue medical humanitarian work. I still wanted to travel. I still wanted to be active.

In January, I was accepted into a clinical trial for immunotherapy.

Before treatment began, I did something that probably sounded slightly unreasonable to the people around me.

I signed up for Ironman 70.3 Hawaii on June 1, 2024.

According to recent reports, I asked my oncologist and the lead investigator of my clinical trial whether I could participate. They told me that I was the first patient they knew of to ask about competing in a half Ironman while undergoing treatment.

In a recent development, they gave me their blessing with one caveat: It would be essential to listen to my body. This was going to be physically taxing on my body due to the cancer already exhausting my body and undergoing treatment in addition to the rigors of training for a 70.3.

In a recent development, I understood the risks. I also understood something else: Training gave me a goal and purpose to keep moving.

Although cancer had taken away my perception of control, it hadn’t taken away my ability to choose a direction.

I arrived in Kona on May 30, 2024. I was nervous and exhausted. I had received treatment the week before and was still recovering from it.

My younger brother, who had agreed to race with me when I asked, and I gathered our swag and attended the informational session. As we were walking out, I saw the iconic walls of all the participants, their bib numbers, and the “why” wall. Seeing my “why” story on the wall solidified my resolve in what I was doing.

The day before the race, I started receiving text messages with their pictures attached, early in the morning, from friends, family, and my whole care team from Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center, wearing a T-shirt that had my cancer ribbon with the words “Fight Cancer Like a Girl” on the front and “Team Rebecca 01” on the back. My amazing husband made nearly 100 shirts and sent them out, asking them to send me a picture and words of encouragement the day before the race. I felt so much love and support from the people in my life.

Recent findings suggest that on June 1, 2024, I stood on the beach waiting for my wave to start at Ironman 70.3 Hawaii. I remember feeling incredibly grateful to be there and have the ability to push my body to the limits.

According to recent reports, the race was hard; the winds were cranking so hard that several cyclists were blown into the lava rocks along the highway. It took some serious grit to keep going, but with my husband and kids driving by with my favorite songs blasting on the stereo, cheering me on, I was able to finish the bike.

By the time I started the run, it was midday, and the sun was searing, with temperatures climbing above 90 degrees. My body was fatigued, and every part of me wanted the race to be done. I dug deep. My mantra was “I can do hard things” on repeat. I kept moving.

During those final miles, rolling thoughts in my head surfaced: If I can fight cancer, I can finish this race.

There was an alteration in my thinking and in the purpose of that day; this was no longer about the race but rather an understanding that I was capable of moving forward.

I crossed the finish line with my brother beside me and my family waiting and cheering. I was overwhelmed by my emotions as I crossed the line.

My body was spent; however, there was something strangely beautiful about that exhaustion. I would rather be exhausted from swimming, cycling, and running than exhausted from lying still, consumed by the knowledge that I have incurable cancer.

Recent findings suggest that my training looks different than it used to. Some days are hard, and my body needs downtime.

I’ve learned that listening to my body isn’t a weakness, or even optional at times, but rather a way for me to keep up the fight.

With every step I take, every mile I cycle, every lap that I swim, it is more than just training; it serves as a reminder that my body is still mine and truly a gift to be cherished.

In a recent development, my cancer diagnosis has altered my relationship with time. I functioned at a faster pace and was always thinking ahead about what was next: the next race, the next degree, the next goal, the next item to add to my list.

Sources indicate that I am more focused on the mile that I am in right now. I have not stopped making aims; I just hold them differently.

My desires to work, travel, race, and serve others remain, but their priority and intensity are more flexible, as my health and energy can be fluid.

This diagnosis has shifted my perspective – I no longer believe that my worth or value depends on completing every goal I write down.

Some days a win is simply to get out the door. Sometimes it is a slow swim, and the distance may be shorter than planned. Sometimes it is walking instead of running. Sometimes it is resting.

And sometimes, it is standing at a finish line I wasn’t sure I would ever reach.

The trajectory of my life feels unsure and more constrained. However, I know that running, swimming, and cycling are things I can do at the moment, and they make me feel alive.

Honestly, for me, that’s what endurance sport has become. This is not a means of escape from cancer but rather my way of living despite it.

One step, one mile, one breath, I will keep going.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There is a specific kind of vertigo that comes with leaving a movie theater in the middle of the day. The world is suddenly too bright, too loud, and slightly unreal. You have, after all, been inside someone else’s carefully constructed reality for two hours. And then you’re back outside, blinking into the afternoon light, not quite returned to yourself, the movie still clinging to you like perfume. It’s in this particular state that I meet Nia Long for an early lunch in a quiet corner at the Chateau Marmont.

In a recent development, I have just seen Michael (the new Michael Jackson biopic) a month ahead of its April release. I’m still thinking about the film when Long, who plays Jackson family matriarch Katherine Jackson, arrives looking chic but low-key in an oversized blazer, wide-leg jeans, and a Miu Miu baseball cap pulled low. As we ease ourselves into the conversation, I’m struck by the strange doubling effect of the movie vertigo: the woman before me and the woman I have just watched, layered like two transparencies held up to the light.

On screen, Long plays Katherine Jackson with a studied stillness. The first time we see her, watching her boys rehearse, the frame holds on her loving face for just a few beats. She claims almost nothing. She doesn’t have to. Juxtaposed to Colman Domingo’s blustering portrayal of Joe Jackson and Jaafar Jackson’s uncanny performance as his late uncle Michael, Long has found a way to make silence load-bearing. Restraint is the most visible thing in any scene she occupies.

In person she seems the opposite of restrained. She is blunt but also quite warm, with a dry sense of humor and a deep well of emotional intelligence. She is very much a Scorpio. She notices everything. And, in playing Mrs. Jackson (who is still with us at the age of 95), Long has tapped into the part of herself that knows how to let silence do the work. The word she reaches for when she talks about the experience of playing the matriarch—a word she will return to several times during our conversation—is grace.

In a recent development, “There have been moments in my life where I’ve been required to be more graceful than I’ve ever had to be in the past,” she states. “And that requires a sense of really being able to dig deep into some sort of self-examination. Like, what do I stand for? What’s key to me, ultimately, regardless of Hollywood, the noise? And number one, for me personally, my children come before anything. And so I think when you look at Michael’s journey, and you look at Katherine’s journey, the only way you thrive and survive is through a tremendous amount of grace.” She pauses. “What I think I learned from her is that sometimes grace is really quiet.”.

Sources indicate that long occupies a place in our cultural memory that few actors do. She is, for a certain generation, the platonic ideal of ’90s Fine, a phrase that’s not only about beauty or aesthetic but also about a certain feeling. Watching her as Nina in Love Jones or Jordan in The Best Man or Lisa in The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air, you conjure up a place and time and attitude that feels synonymous with Long. Of course, there is the image, and then there is the human sitting across from me, eating her go-to order of salmon with a side of mustard. And as she does, I ask what she thinks about the iconography and the nostalgia that surrounds her.

“My commitment to work is not for accolades or attention, or even to be famous, quite honestly,” she indicates. “But I do think because of my commitment to truth and purpose, there is a thing, and I don’t know what that thing is, that people see in my work. And it makes them feel good. It makes them feel inspired. It makes them feel like they know me.”.

According to recent reports, in a fickle Hollywood landscape that’s even more fickle when it comes to Black actors, Long doesn’t take the longevity and love she’s cultivated for granted. “There's highs and lows,” Long admits. “I’m having a great year, but I don’t know what’s happening next year.”.

According to recent reports, long has starred in several iconic Black films, and she’s always been intentional about how she plays her characters. Much like with the Katherine Jackson role, she creates a version of the person that feels, to her, like something true.

It has been revealed that “The only strategy I have in this game is my bank account. Let’s strategize how we’re going to make money and create generational wealth. That is where I’m strategic.” She laughs, scratches her palm. “My hand just started itching the minute I said money. That’s a good thing. Maybe something’s happening. Something’s coming.”.

Once she’s in it, though, the work becomes something more personal. “I work hard to make sure that when I represent us, it’s not just someone putting their agenda on me. Whether it’s my hair, my makeup, my wardrobe, my lines.”.

Recent findings suggest that now that her eldest son is in his 20s and her youngest son, 14, is old enough to stay home by himself, the actor feels ready to expand in all directions. She wants to continue to produce more films, craft newly introduced stories both behind and in front of the camera. She tells me about a new film she’s just wrapped shooting in New York, Don’t Ever Wonder, a romantic dramedy (“If that even exists anymore”) three years in the making. It will feature her onscreen reunion with Love Jones leading man Larenz Tate. Directed by Eugene Ashe and featuring an ensemble that includes Blair Underwood, Susan Kelechi Watson, and Algee Smith, the film is all about second acts.

“This is not a continuation of Love Jones,” she emphasizes. “This is a continuation of love, and of what happens once you’ve had your kids, they’re off to college, and you’re empty nesters. And that’s kind of where the story begins. There’s a lot of funny and there’s a lot of heartbreak, and I think it’s a really honest story.”.

In a recent development, in talking to Long, I get the sense that honesty and truth is what she values most in the stories she tells. It’s what she values in life as well. Perhaps that’s what compels me, somewhere in the middle of our lunch, to unmask. I mention that I am conducting the interview a little out of sorts, having just ended a 12-year relationship.

“Okay, but when was it really over?” she asks.

"You didn’t have to gag me like that!" I say.

She laughs. I tell her that I am trying to imagine what life will look like—what I will look like—on the other side of this break-up. That’s when the idea of grace comes up again.

In 2022, Long went through that peculiar part of fame where something private becomes public overnight: her partner’s cheating scandal that resulted in the end of their 13-year relationship. She doesn’t have to go too deep into it if she doesn’t want to, I assure her, but the actor doesn’t shy away. On the other side of the experience with her ex, with whom she now has a healthy coparenting relationship, she has an unflinching clarity about the whole ordeal.

“The amount of pouring into myself that I’ve done is strong and mighty and intentional. I’ve now identified the things that I need to work on and the things that I need to heal. But I have also identified what is intolerable.”.

According to recent reports, that clarity has been hard-won. When the cheating scandal happened, there was a groundswell of support from fans, a protectiveness over Long as a woman and as a cultural touchstone. But in the instances that she’s talked publicly about it, including in our conversation, I’m struck by how her gratitude for the support is always tempered with nuance.

It has been revealed that “I’m proud of myself for giving so much grace. For being able to say people make mistakes and things happen. It’s life. When the stakes are high, the news is substantial. I can’t do anything about that, but I don’t have to protect my ego in any of this.” She says all this very matter-of-factly, which is the only way she seems capable of saying things.

It has been revealed that in the same straightforward tone she suggests I write out everything I need to say to my ex without sending it, because ultimately “it’s not about another person’s behavior. It’s about your bottom line and the magnitude in which you’re committed to self-love,” she indicates. “I don’t think it's healthy to hold onto things because then you’re just walking around with this burdensome energy. It could be writing it down. It could be meditation. It could be prayer. There’s a lot of ways to manage the noise. But you don’t have to respond to the noise with the undercurrent of your own trauma.”.

I write down this last sentence because it is useful, but also because it is the key to something I’ve been watching Long do across the whole of our conversation: find the lesson in whatever she is given.

In a recent development, long is working on her first memoir, a process she describes as one of the “biggest, bravest, challenging” things she’s ever done. It’s been a two-year process, a constant negotiation with her own relationship to letting go.

In a recent development, “I can read something I wrote two years ago and go: ‘Oh no, that’s not actually how I feel about that now.’” Long’s father, Doughtry Long Jr., a poet who died in 2020, told her the hardest thing about writing is knowing when to stop. “And I’m like: When is that going to happen? Because I haven’t gotten there yet.”.

Recent findings suggest that the memoir takes her back to Iowa City, where she spent six years of her childhood while her mother attended university. She was born in Brooklyn, in a Trinidadian household where everyone on the block was Black. Living in the Midwest during her formative years, she encountered few other Black girls, which disoriented her relationship to race.

Industry observers note that “In writing this memoir, I realized the impact that experience had on my own view of beauty,” she claims. “And my own self-acceptance of being a pretty brown-skinned little girl growing up in Iowa. I thought I was beautiful because my mother said it and my family said it, but the world told me something different.” She lets that sit. “So to now be a face for Estée Lauder, it’s kind of ironic, because I didn’t feel beautiful until Black Hollywood said I was beautiful.”.

According to recent reports, that an entire generation of Black women found a reflection of Black beauty in Nia Long while Long herself was still waiting to see it tells us something about how beauty standards work, and how much labor goes into transforming them. Nineties Fine, after all, did not emerge from a vacuum. It was a corrective, Black Hollywood’s answer to a century of the larger industry rendering Black women invisible or, worse, making us visible in ways that were wholly out of our control. Long’s most iconic characters—and indeed, Long herself—reflected a new idea of beauty, of the Black leading lady, expansive in some ways and still restrictive in others. Now, some 30 years on, Long embodies a new facet of being a Black woman in Hollywood.

“Black don’t crack” gets lobbed at Black women constantly, ostensibly as a compliment, but one that sometimes erases the very real pressure that comes with aging—especially aging on a public stage, especially when people have a particular image of you stored in amber.

In a recent development, but Long is not interested in pretending that the body is not a thing that transforms. “I’m 55. I got hormonal stuff going. Your body shifts, changes. It’s a whole new body.” She is not wistful about this. She also ate the truffle parmesan fries and does not appear remotely conflicted about it. She mentions the coming press tour for Michael, how she wants to be in beautiful gowns but she also wants French fries.

“I don’t deprive myself of anything that I want,” she says. “I find the balance.”.

Beauty was never her primary currency, she states. It had to be something else, other inheritances: her father’s curiosity, her mother’s fierce self-possession. Tattooed and free-spirited, her mother wore leg warmers in the middle of summer because they matched her outfit, and she did not care for one second what anyone thought about that. Embarrassed, Long would beg her mother to take them off. She never did. As an adult, Long sees the power and freedom in that.

Our plates are carted away. Long has to leave soon for a pizza party at home with her youngest son and his friends. Before she goes, I ask her what freedom, at this point, is to her.

Sources indicate that “Being able to do what you want to do when you want to do it, because it serves your spirit, not what everyone else thinks you need to be or should be,” she states. That type of freedom, Long adds, doesn’t require an audience.“You don’t have to have anyone else’s permission to do what you love. And it doesn’t have to be on the substantial stage. It could be in your kitchen. I know I have freedom right now to make a pizza. I’m going to do it.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that architecture is commonly examined through its visible form, materials and spatial organisation. The physical fabric of a building can also retain evidence of events and alterations that are not apparent from its present appearance. Cracks, repairs and structural changes may indicate when and how a building was modified, while photographs and material fragments can provide further evidence about the circumstances surrounding those changes. Forensic investigation examines these traces, using the built environment and its surrounding records to establish how particular events, alterations or failures occurred.

One prominent example is Forensic Architecture, an interdisciplinary research agency based at Goldsmiths, University of London. Working across architecture, research, filmmaking, science and legal investigation, the agency examines contested events and human rights violations. Its investigations bring together architectural models, satellite imagery, photographs, video footage, physical evidence and witness testimony. Architectural methods are used here to examine existing spaces and reconstruct events that have taken place within them.

Industry observers note that existing buildings often contain evidence of successive alterations and repairs. Changes in masonry, structural additions and layers of later finishes can record how a building has been modified over time. Differences in brickwork, inserted structural members or paint layers beneath later finishes can help establish the sequence of these changes. Compared with historical drawings and photographs, such details can indicate when different parts of a building were constructed, replaced or altered.

Recent findings suggest that the US National Park Service's Preservation Brief 35: Understanding Old Buildings – The Process of Architectural Investigation sets out an approach that combines historical research with the physical examination and documentation of a building. Written records, maps, photographs and oral accounts are considered alongside the building itself. A historical document may establish when an alteration took place; examination of the physical fabric can then reveal how it was constructed and what earlier material it replaced.

Historical photographs and maps can be compared with surviving structures and street patterns, while residents' accounts can help establish how particular spaces have been occupied and used. The evidence therefore needs to be considered at the scale at which the event or transformation took place.

According to recent reports, the investigation of the Beirut Port Explosion on 4 August 2020 illustrates how separate visual records can be assembled into a spatial reconstruction. Working with the Egyptian publication Mada Masr, Forensic Architecture examined photographs and videos recorded from different parts of Beirut to reconstruct the sequence of events at Warehouse 12.

The investigation of the Beirut Port Explosion on 4 August 2020 illustrates how separate visual records can be assembled into a spatial reconstruction. Working with the Egyptian publication Mada Masr, Forensic Architecture examined photographs and videos recorded from different parts of Beirut to reconstruct the sequence of events at Warehouse 12.

Investigators geolocated individual videos and plotted each camera's field of view against a three-dimensional model of Beirut. Footage without metadata was synchronised by comparing changes in the shape and movement of the smoke plumes. The analysis identified four separate plumes emerging from different parts of the warehouse over approximately fourteen minutes. Photographs from January 2020 and a video recorded in December 2019 were also used to reconstruct the warehouse interior. This model helped investigators estimate the area occupied by the 2,750 bags of ammonium nitrate.

Industry observers note that the reconstruction depended on establishing where each recording had been made, what it revealed and when it had been recorded. By aligning the footage with earlier images of Warehouse 12, investigators could examine the available visual evidence within a shared spatial and chronological framework. The model provided a means of comparing individual recordings, while the reliability of the reconstruction remained dependent on the quality and context of the underlying material.

Industry observers note that combining recordings requires investigators to establish their authenticity and provenance. Developed by the United Nations Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights and the University of California - Berkeley Human Rights Center, the Berkeley Protocol on Digital Open Source Investigations sets out standards for the identification, collection, preservation and analysis of digital information. It addresses the credibility and authenticity of sources, the context in which material is collected and the safety of those who provide it.

A reconstruction may be geometrically precise while still relying on incomplete records or assumptions that affect its interpretation.

Forensic Architecture used three-dimensional modelling to examine the progression of the Grenfell Tower fire in London. The investigation collected hundreds of videos recorded by residents and members of the public, then positioned the footage on a wireframe model of the tower using projection mapping. Aligning each recording with its camera location and viewpoint allowed investigators to compare the spread of the fire across different parts of the building.

A separate Forensic Architecture project, Situated Testimonies (2024), used three-dimensional models of Grenfell Tower and its surroundings during interviews with eleven people affected by the fire. The participants included survivors, bereaved family members and nearby residents. The models provided spatial references through which they could describe their experiences of that night, and their accounts were considered alongside video and audio evidence.

Sources indicate that the publication of a forensic reconstruction also involves decisions about how evidence is interpreted and presented. A photograph can be authentic yet misleading when separated from its context. A model may show where people, buildings and objects were positioned without explaining the social or institutional conditions surrounding an event. In investigations involving survivors or witnesses to traumatic events, the publication of identifying details or sensitive testimony can create additional risks. The Berkeley Protocol's safeguards for handling sensitive material and protecting sources are relevant to these decisions, particularly when evidence is made publicly accessible.

This places individual buildings within the wider patterns of occupation, activity and change that shape the historic city.

Forensic methods are often associated with investigations of conflict, disasters and human rights violations. Some of the underlying methods of examining physical evidence also have relevance to architectural research and conservation, although the aims of these practices differ. Forensic reconstruction seeks to establish what happened in a particular place and sequence of events. Architectural investigation for conservation examines how a building was constructed, altered and maintained over time. It draws on the physical fabric, construction details and historical documentation to establish the building's development and condition.

Industry observers note that text description provided by the architects. The reconstruction of a century-old farmhouse in the Czech Republic addresses the former disconnect between its living quarters and the surrounding garden while enabling comfortable year-round use. The intervention reverses the arrangement of the building's west wing by establishing a new center of activity within the former barn at the southern end, bringing it closer to natural light and connecting it to the garden. It also introduces a new ground-floor slab that serves as a heat distribution device while simultaneously helping to mitigate excessive ground moisture rising through the load-bearing walls.

#103299. Breaking: How to ‘Quiet Quit’ Your Mom

📅 22 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1470 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Self ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: How to ‘Quiet Quit’ Your Mom

📅 22 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1470 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • You’re probably familiar with the term quiet quitting.
  • Recent findings suggest that the term has since been applied to other parts of life, like relationships.
  • Sources indicate that going low-contact is pretty much what it sounds like: staying in touch with minimal contact.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You’re probably familiar with the term quiet quitting. For a while, that little phrase has been used to describe the experience of executing the bare minimum at work without actually leaving your job: You do just enough to get by but never rise above that benchmark to prove yourself or exceed expectations. It’s a strategy that can keep you employed while preserving your mental and emotional energy.

Recent findings suggest that the term has since been applied to other parts of life, like relationships. And, yes, it could also apply to the one you have with your mom. Though you’re probably not collecting paychecks here, maintaining a relationship with your mother may connect you to vital resources you need to get by. Maybe your mom really does play a big role in your finances, or she’s your source of health insurance. She could also be a connection to your culture or other family members that you don’t want to distance yourself from. Logistics aside, you might just want some distance from your mom without sacrificing your emotional connection. As I learned from reporting my book Motherf*cked: How to Keep Your Mother’s Toxic Drama From Ruining Your Life, those are all solid reasons to maintain a relationship that leaves you exhausted.

Sources indicate that going low-contact is pretty much what it sounds like: staying in touch with minimal contact. However, there’s no official definition, therapist Whitney Goodman, LMFT, told me in an interview for Motherf*cked. For some, it could look like avoiding one-on-one visits but checking in via text, email, quarterly phone calls, or greeting cards. Or you could catch up in person while avoiding the details of your life. The frequency of low-contact contact varies too. Some would say talking once a week is low-contact for them. Others might say once a year.

The reasons why people go low-contact differ as much as the ways it can look. Generally speaking, taking space can be useful anytime a relationship feels painful or draining. It gives you more time, energy, and emotional bandwidth to take care of yourself and tend to other important parts of your life.

It has been revealed that that can be especially helpful in our relationships with our moms, a dynamic that, for many reasons, is often packed with emotional triggers. If spending time with your mom feels exhausting, you’re sick of always stressing about this relationship, or you’ve tried and failed to set boundaries with her in the past, pulling back might be helpful here, Goodman claims. If you can relate, here’s how to do that.

Ideally, this process is a series of experiments where you pull back from the relationship in different ways to see what feels good and what doesn’t, Goodman explains. You can then use that information to determine how much contact is too much—or not enough. Here’s how to get started.

In a recent development, going low-contact is really just setting a boundary, or defining what behavior you will or won’t tolerate. You’re showing others how you want to be treated. Sometimes, people don’t like being restricted and get messy when limits are put on their relationships. Moms can be like that too.

If you’ve already tried to set boundaries with your mom by, say, not answering every one of her calls or telling her that you don’t want to talk about your dating life, now is a good time to reflect on how that went.

Moms who are receptive to those guardrails may be easygoing about any additional boundaries. That could mean you don’t need to cut as many points of contact to feel better about the relationship. On the other hand, if your mom has blown through your boundaries in the past, you might need stronger limitations to protect your peace today. Keep that in mind for the next step.

Again, there is no official criterion defining a low-contact relationship, so don’t get hung up on labels. First, think about how much contact you have now. How often do you spend time together? What does that time look like? What would you change to make this relationship less taxing?

Maybe you see your mom every Sunday, let her come over unannounced, and answer all of her texts—even the ones you’d rather not. Consider which of these interactions take the most out of you, and ask yourself, Would eliminating this point of contact make the relationship less exhausting overall?

In a recent development, you could start small by taking a beat to check in with yourself before responding to your mom’s texts. If you don’t feel like dealing with her at that moment, don’t. If that’s not enough to preserve your energy, maybe you can limit the number of texts you’ll respond to each day or week. You can always change it up later by removing another point of contact, like those unannounced visits, if you need more space (see step five).

You don’t have to formally announce that you’re going low-contact, but giving your mom a heads-up might be useful.

In a recent development, if you’re not worried about your safety and your quiet quitting tactics mean your mom has to change her behavior, then laying out your looks could make sense. Plus, explaining why you put them in place might help you resolve whatever is behind your decision to quiet quit this relationship.

Industry observers note that that stated, if your version of low-contact doesn’t require anything from your mom, you don’t need to tell her it’s happening, states Goodman. For example, you can hold back information about your life or avoid certain events without discussing it first.

Feel weird about this? I get that, but here’s something to think about: You’ve probably told your mom about the ways she’s hurt you many, many times before, says Goodman. Even if you haven’t explicitly pointed to every single occasion she hurt your feelings, your body language and tone of voice likely have conveyed how her actions impacted you. You may be tired of retelling those painful events, which is why you’d like to avoid another confrontation with your mom. So consider this your permission not to.

Still, your mom might notice you pulling back and ask what’s going on. If she does, you can tell her why you’re not getting into your dating life or attending the family reunion. You don’t have to, though. You’re welcome to make excuses or just say, “Yep, you’re right, I’m not doing that anymore.” You don’t owe her an explanation.

Industry observers note that goodman states the best way to tell how going low-contact is working for you is to check in with your emotions as much as possible. You can write them down in your journal, use a mood- or emotions-tracking app, or bring them up to your therapist.

According to recent reports, yes, the feelings you’re tracking can be related to your mom and quiet quitting her, but don’t forget about all the others, indicates Goodman. It might not be obvious which feelings are related to your maternal figure and which aren’t. After breaking patterns that existed for a long time, you might get a sense that something is off. Maybe you feel purposeless or lost. Maybe it’s like you forgot something on your way to the airport, but you don’t know what it is.

All of that is normal, indicates Goodman. So is feeling like you really miss your mom, even if you know you did the right thing. Of course, everyone’s situation is different. Maybe you don’t truly miss her, but miss the idea of a person she’ll never be. When quiet quitting is working, those feelings should come up less frequently and/or become less intense. At the same time, you’ll likely feel some relief. You could notice more peace in your life and more space to focus on things other than your mom.

In a recent development, you can always tweak how much contact you have with your mom. Ideally, this involves a continuous assessment of what’s working and what’s not. If the low-contact initiative you’ve established feels sustainable and makes you less obsessive or overwhelmed by the relationship—and your mom is able to abide by your rules—you might have found a solution. Success!

If this version of quiet quitting doesn’t keep your mom from violating your boundaries, emotionally manipulating you, or still leaves you drained, anxious, or depressed, you could level up, states Goodman. That means starting back at step one and quitting other parts of your relationship until you reach a point that feels sustainable.

Remember, the goal is for you to feel less stressed about your interactions with your mom. By finding a routine that works for you, you can protect the parts of your relationship that you love and lose the rest.

  • Sources indicate that the yin yoga pose we love to hate, Dragon Pose, is a smart recovery tool for cyclists to improve hip extension.
  • According to recent reports, the low torso angle on a tri-specific bike provides aerodynamic benefits, but also requires greater hip flexion.
  • Dragon Pose is useful for triathletes who spend a lot of time folded over the handlebars during indoor training through the winter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the yin yoga pose we love to hate, Dragon Pose, is a smart recovery tool for cyclists to improve hip extension. Because cycling involves repetitive hip flexion at the top of the pedal stroke, the primary hip flexor muscle (psoas major) can tighten and become compressed over time, making it harder to access a powerful position off the bike.

According to recent reports, the low torso angle on a tri-specific bike provides aerodynamic benefits, but also requires greater hip flexion. In the aero position, the hip flexors, which not only flex the hip but also stabilize the pelvis and lower back, repeatedly contract without fully extending, shortening the muscles and potentially leading to low back pain and stiffness.

Dragon Pose is useful for triathletes who spend a lot of time folded over the handlebars during indoor training through the winter. It can also help you during the warmer months by restoring hip extension and preparing you for the longer stride that running off the bike demands. On the run, you repeatedly load one leg as the hip extends behind the body. Dragon Pose simulates that position, so you step off the bike feeling ready to hit your running stride.

It has been revealed that add Dragon Pose to your recovery routine. Practice this pose after a training ride or race to stretch the hip flexors and improve hip mobility.

It has been revealed that keep in mind that multiple bike fit factors affect hip angle and comfort. This guide provides five elements of a proper bike fit for smoother pedaling and to keep your position within your comfortable hip flexion range.

Improving hip extension can help you feel less compressed on the bike, move more easily through transitions, and ease low-back discomfort.

Surrogacy Nearly Destroyed Our Marriage. It Also Brought Us Back

📅 22 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1778 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • From the outside, our relationship looked the way it had for 24 years: solid.
  • According to recent reports, after our first surrogacy experience ended in stillbirth, our friends were convinced we’d be fine because we were the “most together couple” they knew.
  • It has been revealed that it felt like we were suspended in the quiet between the cracks and the crumble.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From the outside, our relationship looked the way it had for 24 years: solid.

According to recent reports, after our first surrogacy experience ended in stillbirth, our friends were convinced we’d be fine because we were the “most together couple” they knew. I wasn’t so sure. For months, it had felt like my husband Ethan and I were two bodies fumbling to find each other in the dark. At home, our orbits rarely intersected. My eyes barely landed on Ethan. Once, he didn’t realize I was right behind him and he closed the door on me.

It has been revealed that it felt like we were suspended in the quiet between the cracks and the crumble. We weathered life-altering challenges together in our 20s and 30s due to my whole-body symptoms from endometriosis, adenomyosis, early menopause, and a medical system that trivialized them all. My condition rattled our intimacy, upended my career, and made Ethan my caretaker. Being undiagnosed for decades also cost us my fertility, depleting my ovarian reserve and leading to miscarriage after miscarriage with IVF and IUIs.

Though we weren’t living the life we dreamed, and I felt guilty for the weight I foisted on Ethan, we managed to maintain the joie de vivre we’d had since we first met—until we turned to surrogacy.

Industry observers note that our decision to opt for an egg donor and a surrogate was an act of compromise. Though I’d always been ambivalent about motherhood, the idea of coparenting with Ethan had gradually filled me with tenderness and curiosity. But by then, after years of illness, I wanted a hysterectomy. Ethan still really wanted to be a dad. Neither of us wanted to jeopardize my wellness with more hormonal treatments and pregnancy losses, so we took what people called the “easy way out.” Though I was criticized by my doctors for giving up on my eggs and my uterus “too soon,” our decision to pursue surrogacy felt liberating—at first.

It has been revealed that we thought finding a gestational surrogate would be the hardest part. Turns out, we were wrong. Instead, we were totally unprepared for the ways surrogacy was going to change our marriage.

Our first surrogacy experience was the kind we now caution other intended parents against. We entrusted an agency with our fate and our funds, putting them in charge of introducing us to a surrogate and acting as the intermediary who would reimburse her for pregnancy-related expenses on our behalf. At the time, we were unaware of their proven fraudulent history.

It has been revealed that not only were Ethan and I fresh to surrogacy, but we also felt vulnerable—maybe even desperate. We were privileged to have found someone who wanted to do this for us, and we wanted to be generous and grateful. You also don’t have much control when your baby is in someone else’s womb and your funds are in a corporation’s bank account. So we ignored the red flags we noticed with the agency’s inflated reimbursements and our surrogate’s jarring mood fluctuations.

Industry observers note that if we’d shared our worries with each other early on, we may have had a chance to course-correct. At least I wouldn’t have felt so alone carrying this angst in my bones. At one of our second-trimester ultrasounds, I resented Ethan for being his jovial self while he talked to our active baby boy through the screen as I stood hunched against the wall, struggling to feel present. It wasn’t just that the pregnancy felt unbearably abstract for me as a mother who didn’t contribute her genes or her womb; I was also increasingly skeptical of the agency and walking on eggshells with our surrogate, who’d keep us at arm’s length one week and accuse us of not being supportive enough the next. I’d never gotten this far in a pregnancy and it should have been a happy time. Instead, I bottled up my distress and couldn’t breathe from the weight of it.

It has been revealed that during our first surrogacy experience, Ethan let me bear the brunt of the conversations with our surrogate. He thought he had a supportive role, but his not being in the foreground put extra weight on my shoulders and took my time, energy, and headspace while sparing him. I was also the one who handled all the legal and financial paperwork, and the communication with the agency. Ethan was grateful and proud of me for managing what he considered more in my wheelhouse than his, but I felt paralyzing stress and resentment having to tackle these hard tasks on my own at such a vulnerable time.

Recent findings suggest that our breaking point was brought on by our different ways of grieving. While I naturally tend to dig deep into painful topics and emotions to make sense of them, Ethan prefers to compartmentalize. At the hospital after the delivery, Ethan preferred to leave the room when I stayed to spend a few minutes with our stillborn. I wanted the loss to feel more tangible, while he wanted to hold onto the joy from other memories, like when we saw him on ultrasounds. Neither of us was wrong, but we were disconnected.

The months that followed were agony because none of the doctors would counsel us on why our baby had died simply because I wasn’t the pregnant patient, as though we weren’t his parents and didn’t have the right to know. I spiraled into depression and was furious every time Ethan would tell his parents that we were fine. He didn’t want to burden them, but I didn’t want to mask our reality for the sake of others’ comfort. For 24 years—through long distance, sickness, and grief—we’d been the “strong couple” who never argued. Now, in the complexity of surrogacy, we kept snapping at each other because Ethan needed a semblance of normalcy and I needed to dwell in darkness.

So how do you come back to each other when who you were didn’t survive? Over nearly a year, thanks to our self-awareness, deep respect for one another, and therapy (which Ethan hated attending but did when required), we made three tiny shifts that saved our marriage.

According to recent reports, when we met our second surrogate through a more ethical, transparent, and supportive agency that did not demand funds in trust, Ethan and I formed a true trio with her. It helped that she considered us a team and wanted our involvement in appointments, decisions, and her daily life. She’d use the word “together” so often that it initially triggered us; it felt so foreign to us after our first surrogacy journey, and we couldn’t tell which of the two experiences was the anomaly. Ethan made it a priority to participate in our conversations and replied to our group texts if I couldn’t. We all shared freely—our fears, dreams, victories, recipes, and silly inside jokes—and the three of us built an intimacy I never expected. When it was just the two of us, our surrogate was never far from our thoughts, as if our marriage had expanded to include her.

Sources indicate that ethan also started to help me with the challenging legal and financial tasks. He kept up with emails he was CC’ed on during the day and sat with me if we had paperwork to tackle, his hand on my back if I got overwhelmed.

When we lost our baby with our second surrogate at the end of the first trimester, we grieved as a unit. Our trio sat intertwined, our hands piled on my lap. At home, Ethan was more receptive to my needs on my bad days. Just watching him witness me in those moments, even if all he did was listen and sigh, brought us closer together. I was more understanding when he clung to his social activities to blow off steam. Ethan was more honest with family and friends about our emotional and financial distress. He agreed to ask for help and for a loan to help us get back on our feet after two surrogacy journeys and thirteen years of fertility and ongoing health expenses.

We decided not to talk about surrogacy on weekends or right before bed to give our nervous systems a chance to unwind. Dark humor helped us grieve: We’d sometimes whisper jaded comments to each other when triggered. When we imagine something creative we would have done with our kid, we say, “File it under never!” During the holidays, Ethan toasted me with, “Cheers to not losing a child this Christmas!” Holding space for our contrasting ways of grieving and meeting in the middle helped dissolve the resentment and tension between us.

Fertility treatments and surrogacy can become all-consuming for a couple, especially after decades of illness and loss. Being diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) after our first surrogacy experience further shook my identity. We started making a conscious effort to remember what was special about our life and our love before all this. We are more than what we carry and what we’ve lost.

Besides carving out periods of play, nature, and grief-free talk, we also pushed ourselves to keep money aside for leisure and travel—not just for our living expenses and surrogacy costs—so we can look forward to something in our calendar and savor new experiences together.

We found, though, that the least daunting way of rebuilding our future is to simply take care of our present. Often, all we can handle is the next half-hour: where to take a walk, what to make for supper, how to support each other right then. I worked hard to keep my eyes focused on Ethan until it became natural again. Even now, as we grapple with whether and how to continue with our surrogacy journey, when we start acting like passing ships because of our full heads and aching hearts, we drop everything, hug, touch.

I never expected our strong marriage to be impacted by the most tender gift we gave each other: the chance to grow our family through surrogacy. We’d naively thought what awaited us would be easier than the road that led there. Our experiences with surrogacy have changed how we show up for each other, both in joy and in grief.

Industry observers note that I can’t say for certain that our marriage is now strong enough to survive anything that lies ahead. What I know is this: We’ve built what we’ll need to recalibrate our direction to find each other in the dark.

3 Signs You’re the ‘Fringe Friend’ of Your Group, According to a Psychologist

📅 22 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (883 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that welcome to Asking for a Friend, a weekly series dedicated to solving the messy, awkward, and confusing parts of modern friendship.
  • Technically, you’re part of a friend group…well, loosely speaking.
  • You’re there for big, public-facing plans—birthday parties, girls’ trips, anything that benefits from a larger headcount—yet absent from spontaneous happy hours and nights out where real bonding happens and the inside jokes are born.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that welcome to Asking for a Friend, a weekly series dedicated to solving the messy, awkward, and confusing parts of modern friendship. Because the truth is, our platonic relationships are often the most complicated. Send us your friendship dilemmas here, and we might feature one in a future column.

Technically, you’re part of a friend group…well, loosely speaking. You’re in the chats. You receive the invites, but usually ones that sound like “Oh, but you can come if you want”...which, the more you think of it, lands less like inclusion and more like a pity afterthought.

You’re there for big, public-facing plans—birthday parties, girls’ trips, anything that benefits from a larger headcount—yet absent from spontaneous happy hours and nights out where real bonding happens and the inside jokes are born.

If any of this hits close to home, you might be what some people call the backup or “fringe friend.”.

We can’t all be everyone’s number one. But what makes this situation so hard is that there’s no obvious villain and no dramatic fallout (which, in some ways, would almost be easier to deal with). Instead, you’re left with a low-grade, hard-to-prove insecurity: Am I just…no one’s first choice? I’m their friend…but are they mine?

For this week’s column, SELF tapped Christina Ferrari, PsyD, a Miami-based psychologist to break down three clear signs you’re a second-tier “backup friend.”.

Not occasionally. Consistently.

Industry observers note that as in, you hear about each plan the day of. You’re added to existing dinner reservations only after somebody else has cancelled. Of course, this might be a matter of logistics or innocent forgetfulness, which is why “every now and then, it’s not cause for concern,” Dr. Ferrari tells SELF. People who are disorganized across the board also exist. “So if this is how they are with all of their friends, that might reflect more about their poor planning”—annoying in its own way, but ultimately a separate issue. The point is, pay attention to the pattern if you can recall more than a few instances.

A few of these tells are subtle yet revealing. Somehow, get-togethers conveniently skip the messy, in-between stage of coordination (“Does 7 work?” “Where should we go?”), arriving at you fully formed. Or, in person, everyone references memes, messages, or memories that clearly happened…just not in any chat you’re in.

Recent findings suggest that “It's totally normal for people to have multiple friendships and separate interactions,” Dr. Ferrari points out. “This isn’t about being included in everything.” Still, paying attention to how often this occurs makes it easier to understand “why you feel like you’re constantly stepping into something already established rather than being part of it from the beginning,” Dr. Ferrari explains.

According to recent reports, “Life, of course, can get busy, and a temporary imbalance is normal,” Dr. Ferrari says. But when you’re truly in the crew, your absence will be missed or, at the very least, acknowledged. Someone will notice: “Wait, where have you been?” “I haven’t seen you in forever.” “We never see you anymore.” “Let’s catch up.”.

In a recent development, there’s usually, in other words, a small moment of recognition—an indication that you exist in their shared awareness when you’re not physically present, which is why when you don’t get any of those little check-ins, it’s disorienting. It’s as if you’re not crucial enough to be missed.

According to recent reports, bring it up, and you risk sounding insecure. Say nothing, and you’ll continue to overanalyze every delayed invite, every inside joke, and every Instagram story you weren’t tagged in.

None of the options above sounds appealing. Though if you do want to say something, Dr. Ferrari recommends a low-pressure check-in like: “I always have such a great time when we all hang out. Next time, I'd love to be looped in!” It’s warm, subtle, and assumes good intent—the kind of communication that makes your intentions clear without putting anyone on the defensive. But in ambiguous situations like these—where your gut is whispering that something’s off, yet no one is technically doing you wrong—even the most carefully crafted messages can’t give you the reassurance (or confidence) you’re seeking.

In a recent development, that’s why the solution isn’t necessarily, “How do I become a core member of this group?” Dr. Ferrari states, but instead: “Am I spending my energy where I actually feel like I matter?”.

It has been revealed that nobody deserves to feel disposable with people they care about most. And it’s worth remembering that not being fully “in” in one circle doesn’t mean you’re inherently less than, which is where a different solution comes in: Expand your social network instead of over-investing in your current one.

According to recent reports, in other words, go out of your comfort zone and start weekly lunches with your favorite coworker. Finally say yes to that old high school companion you’ve been meaning to reach out to but haven’t prioritized. Agree to that weekend trip with friends-of-friends instead of defaulting to your usual group or staying in.

Sometimes, all it takes is noticing the spaces where you’re truly welcome to ease the ache of feeling like the “unimportant” one.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Magnus Ditlev of Denmark wins the 2026 IRONMAN Florida in a World Record Time of 7:19:17 on November 7, 2026 in Panama City, Florida.
  • One month after a heartbreaking DNF in Kona, Magnus Ditlev (DEN) rode away from the field at Ironman Florida and never looked back.
  • Florida was a chance at redemption for Ditlev, who had come agonizingly close to winning the Ironman World Championship in Kona.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Magnus Ditlev of Denmark wins the 2026 IRONMAN Florida in a World Record Time of 7:19:17 on November 7, 2026 in Panama City, Florida. (Photo by Donald Miralle/Getty Images for IRONMAN) (Photo: Getty Images for IRONMAN).

One month after a heartbreaking DNF in Kona, Magnus Ditlev (DEN) rode away from the field at Ironman Florida and never looked back. His 7:19:17 took 1:47 off the previous men’s iron-distance world best that Sam Laidlow (FRA) set at Challenge Roth earlier this year.

Florida was a chance at redemption for Ditlev, who had come agonizingly close to winning the Ironman World Championship in Kona. He’d taken the lead late on the bike and looked on course for the win until he abruptly came to a stop on the run with roughly 30 minutes of racing left.

Industry observers note that however, ahead of Kona, Ditlev said he was putting up career-best numbers across the swim, bike, and run at his training camp in Colorado. In Florida, he finally got to reap the rewards of what fitness could produce all the way to the finish line.

Ditlev came out of the water in fifth, right on the heels of Ben Kanute (USA) and Rudy von Berg (USA). He took his time in T1 and started the bike nearly a minute down, but it didn’t take him long to ride back to the front. And then, just past mile 10, he made his move. No one could go with him, and they wouldn’t be able to stay remotely close to him either.

By the time Ditlev came off the bike, he was 11 minutes clear of a chase group that included Sam Long (USA), von Berg, and Kanute. His 3:51:16 was the fastest bike split ever recorded at an Ironman, nearly two minutes quicker than the 3:53:12 Robert Kallin (SWE) rode at Ironman Kalmar in August.

Off the bike, he once again took his time in transition. But transitions were the only slow part of Ditlev’s day. Once through T2, he picked up another minute on the chasers over the opening 10 miles. He hit halfway in 1:15, on pace for a 2:30 marathon and well within reach of Laidlow’s 7:21:04. With such an unassailable lead, one can assume he must’ve known the record was within reach to keep such an aggressive pace.

Ditlev eventually closed with a 2:33:31 marathon, crossing the line in 7:19:17. Von Berg took second, 14 minutes back, securing the early Kona slot and podium he’d come for. Matt Hanson (USA), meanwhile, ran a remarkable 2:28:07 to beat Long to the final podium spot, but still finished 16 minutes behind Ditlev.
