  • Sources indicate that when shopping for fresh road and gravel helmets, cyclists often base their choices almost entirely on looks, price, and overall comfort.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

As a cyclist for over three decades, I’ve crashed many times. Unfortunately, I’ve also had a few concussions. Because of this, safety is important to me when I choose a newly introduced helmet. Over the last few seasons, I’ve tested dozens of great helmets, from budget picks under $50 to go-fast aero lids and lightweight models for over $500. Plus, I also test trail helmets, commuter lids, and everything in between.

Sources indicate that when shopping for fresh road and gravel helmets, cyclists often base their choices almost entirely on looks, price, and overall comfort. Depending on our riding goals and budget, we also balance weight, aerodynamics, and style. We want safety features, but many riders assume most helmets do a decent job of protecting our noggin—they’re all certified, right?

According to recent reports, helmet safety isn’t as straightforward as it may seem. Current Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) standards—as well as more rigorous, voluntary requirements, such as those from ASTM—account for straight-line impacts and G-forces from a collision. These standards don’t address the rotational forces from a crash that contribute significantly to concussions and traumatic brain injuries. Plus, the CPSC’s standards took effect on March 10, 1999—advancements in technology, design, materials, and manufacturing over the last 27 years have changed bike helmets.

So, what standards and certifications cover rotational forces? At the moment, none. To better protect against rotational forces and reduce concussions, many brands incorporate Mips liners (and similar anti-rotational designs) into their helmets. Brands also test their helmets internally to their own, generally unpublished, criteria. The Virginia Tech helmet lab’s STAR score provides the best independent testing and ranking for helmets across most cycling disciplines.

Virginia Tech tests helmets for safety; it doesn’t evaluate fit, comfort, weight, price, or overall practicality. Bicycling’s test team collectively rides tens of thousands of miles each year on tarmac, gravel roads, singletrack, and commuting. That means we have a lot of time to ride-test lids—including more than half of Virginia Tech’s 5-STAR-rated road helmets.

For 15 years, Virginia Tech has tested helmets through a battery of 24 impact tests that analyse safety performance and assign an overall STAR (Summation of Tests for the Analysis of Risk) score.

In a recent development, “The overall score estimates the number of concussions the average person would see if they experienced identical impacts at rates matching their weightings while cycling,” says Virginia Tech’s lab. The lower the STAR score, the better a helmet performed in testing.

Then, to each helmet it tests, Virginia Tech awards an overall STAR rating (one through five); helmets with four- and five-STARs are “recommended.” The lab does not recommend helmets scoring three STARs or fewer.

Industry observers note that virginia Tech has tested and published results on more than 300 bicycle helmets. To date, the lab has awarded 56 helmets its coveted 5-STAR rating, and another 104 received 4 STARs. To make researching and choosing a newly introduced helmet easier, it also sorts the helmets it tests into mountain, road, urban, multi-sport, full-face, and E-bike categories. Of the 5-STAR helmets, 21 of them are road lids.

In a recent development, editor’s Note: These helmets are the top 5-rated road bike helmets in Virginia Tech’s bicycle helmet rankings as of November 9, 2026. The Virginia Tech helmet lab regularly tests helmets and updates the overall rankings; the top 5 can change at any time. Please consult Virginia Tech’s bicycle helmet ranking list for up-to-date rankings.

“Who is Pikio?” and “What is a Si Oblik?” Those were the questions our editors all asked when we saw this helmet rocket to the top of Virginia Tech’s STAR ratings. The Pikio isn’t only the top-rated road helmet; it’s also Virginia Tech’s best-performing helmet, period. It beats the others by a considerable margin, logging an unbelievably low 4.61 STAR score. For context, the difference between the Pikio and the second-place overall Canyon Deflectr RLS mountain bike helmet is 2.21 points; that’s the same gap between the 2nd and 28th positions in current rankings.

It has been revealed that all of that safety comes at a relatively steep $379 cost. While the Si Oblik’s price aligns with other range-topping helmets from Giro, POC, Specialized, and MET, Pikio’s looks and finish feel comparable to mid-tier models from more well-known brands. For example, Pikio’s color options are somewhat conservative choices, and the rear strap anchor point is through-shell.

In a recent development, the Si Oblik fits well and has a broad range of adjustment for my medium-sized head. The rear adjusts up and down (to account for head shape and hairstyles) and features a dial to microadjust fit. The straps, however, are not as cleanly executed as expected for the price, especially compared to POC or Specialized, and I found them slightly tedious to adjust. On road and gravel rides, the Si Oblik’s airflow doesn’t feel bad, but I didn’t test this lid in peak summer heat. And while the Pikio weighs about the same as Giro and MET helmets in this test, it feels physically bigger, though not as mushroomy as the POC Cytal.

In a recent development, for a new brand, Pikio Labs made a solid first effort. Unlike its competitors, Pikio doesn’t have decades of trial and error or a flashy WorldTour team. Hopefully, as the company grows, it can dial in details, sharpen pricing, and spice up the aesthetic, because the Si Oblik already sets a very high bar for safety.

The POC Cytal’s unique shape and bold look make it easy to spot in a peloton. Another reason the Cytal stands out is due to its overall size—it’s a physically big lid. But despite its dimensions and slightly heavy weight, it doesn’t feel that large on your head while riding and ventilates surprisingly well.

Recent findings suggest that the Cytal’s great ventilation comes from its massive vents and internal air channels that funnel air directly over your forehead while riding. I found out how well it vents while riding over the summer in France during “la canicule” (the heatwave). I could still feel the Cytal pushing air in 100-degree temps, even if it was roasting hot.

Recent findings suggest that in our recent review of P2R’s $100 aero-helmet, ride tester Tom Messina remarked it “has no business being this good.” And with its lower price and STAR score, we say the same thing about P2R’s $60 A20 Mips. With its excellent safety rating, great adjustability, and budget-friendly price, the A20 Mips outperforms many helmets that cost three, four, or even five times its price.

P2R somehow hits the A20’s low price without cutting corners on features. It has nice straps with adjustable quick clamps that offer plenty of adjustment. P2R also includes a USB-rechargeable light that magnetically clips into the rear vent for commuting or extra visibility on the road.

The one downside we found with the A20 Mips is that it feels optimized for rounder head shapes. While it fits me well, a couple of others who tried it on mentioned it was a little snug near their temples.

Given the Trenta 3K Carbon’s pedigree, it’s hard not to name it “Best for Racing.” UAE Team Emirates’ official sponsor is MET, and the Trenta is one of the helmets it supplies to the squad—including Tour de France champion Tadej Pogačar and World Champion Brandon McNulty. While UAE riders often race the Italian brand’s Manta aero helmet, they sometimes pick the lightweight, well-ventilated Trenta 3K Carbon for climbing stages and training.

In a recent development, unlike some modern helmets with similarly strong protection, the Trenta feels light and racey on your head, and almost disappears when you’re riding. The straps offer good adjustability, and the Mips Air Node liner protects without feeling bulky. However, the Trenta’s biggest drawback is its price tag. At over $500, this is an expensive piece of kit.

Ranked 14th overall and 5th in road helmets, Giro’s Aries Spherical stands out in our testing for its overall comfort, adjustability, low weight, and great looks. While its STAR score is much higher than the first-place Pikio, the Aries is a very safe helmet and received Virginia Tech’s 5-STAR rating. Having crashed on the road while wearing an Aries Spherical, I also know this helmet works.

Industry observers note that of the approximately one dozen road and gravel helmets in my rotation at any given time, I reach for the Aries Spherical most often. The Aries fits my head perfectly, and the Roc Loc dial system offers plenty of adjustability for hair length or if I’m wearing a cap underneath in rain or cold weather. Giro makes the Aries in a wide range of colors and graphics to fit almost any rider’s personality or fashion.

In a recent development, as Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

#103215. Is Your Cycling Computer Lying to You?

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1281 w)

Is Your Cycling Computer Lying to You?

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1281 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that spend enough time comparing power meters, and you’ll rapidly learn that they don’t always agree.
  • If you use a power meter for training, what matters most is that the numbers you’re seeing today are comparable to the ones you saw last week or last month.
  • But what if your power meter isn’t the only thing affecting those numbers?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that spend enough time comparing power meters, and you’ll rapidly learn that they don’t always agree. Put a power meter on your crank and another on your pedals, and the numbers may not match exactly. That can be frustrating when you’re trying to figure out which one is right, but for most riders, a small, consistent difference isn’t necessarily a problem.

If you use a power meter for training, what matters most is that the numbers you’re seeing today are comparable to the ones you saw last week or last month. Whether your threshold is actually 250 watts or 255 watts matters less than knowing that an interval at that power represents the same effort from one ride to the next.

But what if your power meter isn’t the only thing affecting those numbers? What if the bike computer recording your ride is changing the data before you ever upload it to Strava or TrainingPeaks?

I recently noticed something odd while testing a cycling computer. At first, I was doing this to compare GPS track accuracy, but since I was testing, I also paired all the devices to my heart rate strap and Quarq power meter. When I compared the ride files afterward, what stood out was that their power numbers didn’t match. Initially, the differences were small enough. But when I looked more closely, I noticed it immediately. Every time I stopped pedaling, one computer still recorded power.

Before I get into what the heck sticky watts are, I should say I first learned about the issue in 2025 when I saw a video from Shane Miller, who goes by GPLama on YouTube. The video is called “Power Meter Data Recording: The Wild West?”, and it’s worth watching. Shane was the first person I saw digging into this particular recording issue with cycling computers.

Recent findings suggest that so what the heck is it? Sticky watts happen when a cycling computer keeps recording a power value for a few seconds after you’ve stopped pedaling. Instead of dropping to zero, the last power number gets “stuck” in your ride file until the computer finally catches up.

Let’s say you’re riding along at 250 watts and stop pedaling as you approach a corner. Your computer might continue recording 250 watts for a few seconds while you’re coasting. On a graph, that can look like a flat line extending beyond the point where the power should have dropped.

Recent findings suggest that A few seconds might not sound like much, but think about how often you stop pedaling on a typical ride. Every corner, descent, stop sign, or moment spent coasting in the group is another opportunity for those extra watts to show up in your file. And if you stop pedaling after a hard effort, the computer could be holding a much higher number than 250 watts, which can skew your data.

It’s also worth distinguishing this from the setting on some computers that lets you exclude zeroes when calculating average power. That setting changes how an average is calculated. Sticky watts affect the power values recorded in the ride file itself, so those extra values can still be there when you upload the ride for analysis.

On one ride, I compared the DURA 2 with a Garmin Edge 850 and an Edge 1060. The two Garmins recorded almost identical power numbers, but the DURA 2 consistently came out higher. When I looked more closely at the files, I found repeated instances where the COROS continued recording the last power value after both Garmins had dropped to zero.

The difference was especially noticeable during a series of short, hard efforts. After one effort, the DURA 2 recorded 565 watts for four seconds while both Garmins recorded zero. After another, it held 656 watts for three seconds. Across a roughly three-minute section containing several of these efforts, the Garmins averaged about 260 watts, while the COROS recorded nearly 307 watts.

Those short efforts make the issue easy to see, but the difference demonstrated up across the ride, too. In the roughly 98 minutes of matched power data I compared, the DURA 2 averaged about 186 watts, while both Garmins averaged about 179 watts.

On a second ride, I compared the DURA 2 with a Hammerhead Karoo, Wahoo ELEMNT ACE, and Garmin Edge 850. Again, the COROS recorded higher power through a section with several hard efforts followed by coasting. The Garmin recorded lower numbers than the Karoo and Wahoo in that section, which reminds us that differences can go both ways when computers record the same power meter.

Recent findings suggest that I was honestly surprised to see this on the DURA 2. The original DURA had similar issues early on, but its power recording improved with subsequent updates, and it performed well in GPLama’s 2025 video presenting the issue. I don’t want to turn this into a story about picking on COROS. The company has a good history of updating and improving its products, and I expect it can address this issue on the DURA 2 as well. For now, these files show why it’s worth paying attention to what your cycling computer records, even when you trust your power meter.

Recent findings suggest that if you mostly ride for fun and don’t pay much attention to your power data afterward, a few extra watts in your ride file probably won’t change your life. But if you use that data to track your training, compare rides, and work with a coach, those differences can matter.

The significant problem is that sticky watts don’t necessarily add the same amount to every ride. A steady climb with little coasting might show no difference. But a ride with lots of corners, stop signs, descents, or short, hard efforts followed by coasting could produce a much larger one. That makes it harder to compare rides or judge how much work you actually did.

It has been revealed that the easiest way to check is to record the same ride on two cycling computers paired to the same power meter. You don’t necessarily need to buy a second computer. If a friend has one you can borrow, pair both to your power meter and record a ride with a few clear transitions from pedaling to coasting.

Alternatively, you can look closely at the power files your head unit generates. Do a couple of hard efforts, like sprints, where you stop pedaling at the end, then zoom in on those sections. Look for a flat section where one computer continues recording the same power value for several seconds after the other has dropped to zero.

And yes, I know that I’m definitely in some deep weeds over here, and it can be tough to argue that a cycling computer recording a few extra watts is a huge problem worth tackling. For many riders, it might not matter at all. But the current crop of cycling computers is also the most expensive we’ve ever seen. These devices are marketed and sold as precision training tools, and accurate data recording is central to that. These devices should do that, and riders shouldn’t have to question it.

Test Editor Dan Chabanov got his start in cycling as a Newly introduced York City bike messenger but swiftly found his way into road and cyclocross racing, competing in professional cyclocross races from 2009 to 2019 and winning a Master’s National Championship title in 2018. Prior to joining Bicycling in 2021, Dan worked as part of the race organization for the Red Hook Crit, as a coach with EnduranceWERX, as well as a freelance writer and photographer.

Less Cars, More Money: My Visit to the City of the Future

📅 07 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1942 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that in my role as Mr.
  • It has been revealed that but there’s one single area of life where all of these factors come together with an almost Nuclear Fusion level of synergy and effectiveness.
  • That we immediately switch to building our cities and countries around people, instead of cars.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in my role as Mr. Money Mustache, I do my best to be your one-stop-shop for Lifestyle Guru ideas. So over the years we’ve covered not just the Money side of life, but also the even more crucial stuff like health and fitness and the psychology of better, happier living.

It has been revealed that but there’s one single area of life where all of these factors come together with an almost Nuclear Fusion level of synergy and effectiveness. And because of that, if I could have one single wish in the world, this is what I would wish for. It’s a change so massive that it would make every person on the planet better off and fix most of our problems in one grand sweep. And it’s probably not what you’d expect:.

That we immediately switch to building our cities and countries around people, instead of cars.

(and then fix all of our existing ones too, so that our entire world is built around person-friendly living.).

According to recent reports, the benefits of this are way bigger than almost anyone can imagine. We’re not just talking about eliminating a bit of pollution or a few traffic jams or car crashes. No. This is about far richer, healthier, and most importantly more fun living for everyone.

To put even conservative numbers to this, we’re talking about a life boost of over $20,000 per person per year, which compounds into well over two million dollars per adult lifetime.

On a nationwide scale, this would boost the wealth of the United States by about seven trillion dollars per year, which would compound into about 770 trillion over the next five decades.

Which happens to be more than the current total amount of human wealth on the entire planet.

Industry observers note that you will have a house that is both cheaper and more beautiful and spacious. Your body and brain will be healthier and stronger and sexier and cost a lot less time and healthcare dollars to maintain.

And all of our wallets and investment accounts, both public and private will be absolutely overflowing with surplus income, reduced expenses, and fuel an investment and prosperity boom like the world has never seen.

“Isn’t city planning just a stuffy thing that your city council does in the background while we’re all off living our lives?”.

It has been revealed that well, yes it is right now. And that’s the whole problem: cities are built by people whose primary job is to maintain the status quo and prevent disruptions. And those committes are elected and encouraged by crusty old companies and organizations, and plain old grumpy neighbors who just don’t have the vision to see what they are missing.

I’m convinced that if everyone could see through the smoggy haze of the status quo, we would all agree that this idea of a radical change is not only the best idea, but the only reasonable idea to even consider.

So our job is to learn and explain just how big and how easy this is. And what it boils down to is pretty damned simple.

Whoa, that’s a bit of a surprise.

So for the same amount of space you can have an entire pretty nice two bedroom apartment, or you can have just enough space for two (small) cars to park and pull out. But it gets even crazier than this. Check out this random intersection here in my own city:.

WHAT?! So every time you have two big car roads intersect, which happens hundreds of times in every big city, you are wasting enough space to build a luxurious, resort-like living area with about one hundred two-bedroom apartments and still have room for a pool, a dog park, a grocery store, a couple of restaurants, and so on.

This is just the beginning of the insanity, because I have only shown you two parking spaces and one intersection. The reality is that our entire cities are made almost entirely of stupid, expensive wasted space like this.

And the problem is so extreme that the only reason we think we need cars to get around, is because we have wasted most of our space on accommodating cars, which spread everything out so far (and made everything so loud and dangerous) that nobody feels like walking or biking!

Whenever you propose any great new idea, you’ll always get a bunch of smartasses who like to complain and resist change, without even bothering to think it through.

“But how are we going to keep driving our cars just as much as we do now?”.

Which is ridiculous – because the whole point is that as soon as you cut out all the huge wasted spaces we create to accommodate cars, you are suddenly FREE from needing cars so much!

Instead, you can just weave a brand new city, with a bunch of variations of this beautiful resort which also include offices, grocery stores, climbing gyms and every other amenity.

And yes, you’d still have some roads between them, but they would be mostly for deliveries, emergency vehicles and people who need mobility assistance.

I hope you’re not going to make me ride the bus?

I am all for public transit in theory, but to be honest I don’t usually have the patience for it. I don’t do lineups, and I don’t like to stand around waiting passively for my transportation to arrive – when it’s time to go somewhere, I just want to go, and go now, and get there fast. So my own personal choice is to take a bike for short distances (under 2 miles) or an e-bike for larger ones (up to about 15 miles).

Although this is often news to car drivers, bikes are much faster than cars for urban transport, plus they give me exercise and thrill, which is way better than being stuck at the red light with the cars.

If you take this already-superior method of urban transport and cut out the 90% of the land that we waste on accommodating the inferior cars, then you end up with a revolution: everybody gets where they are going ten times faster, at much lower cost, and has much more fun doing it.

In a recent development, and sure, there will also be light rail and faster buses. And sure, you can still hop in an Uber or even bring your own car into a city like this.But the point is that it will just happen much much less often.

Okay I’m convinced, but how can we actually accomplish this?

Industry observers note that mr. Money Mustache can talk a big game with all these fancy words and pictures, but the truth is that I’m way too impatient to put up with all the bureaucracy and complaints that arise when you try to actually change a city. I’ve been doing my best here in Longmont, and I have gotten just about nowhere. We’re still just stacking on more and more layers of ridiculous car shit where I live.

Thankfully, other people are much more patient and effective than I am at affecting change, and one group has made such incredible progress that you can now go LIVE in their first creation: a 1000-person car-free neighborhood called Culdesac Tempe. And as I write this, I am staying in a hotel right nearby, having spent the past two days touring and visiting and interviewing the founders*.

While we were at it, my Phoenix-area-house-fixing friend Tracy Royce and I also hosted a meetup for an enthusiastic group of our readers/viewers right there in Culdesac’s emerging central plaza.

Culdesac is Awesome and Could Change Everything.

In a recent development, if you only look at the financial spreadsheet, you would think this first Culdesac project is just going to be a highly profitable 1000-person cluster of apartment buildings, spread out across 17 acres of land. And while financial sustainability is indeed a key reason why this model will succeed, the money is the least exciting part.

When you look at these pictures compared to a normal housing complex, the main thing you will notice is that all the space that would normally be wasted on parking lots, is instead used for beautiful walking and gathering areas.

The next substantial upgrade is that they mixed in the amenities for daily life right into the neighborhood, rather than forcing all the future residents to get into their cars to drive out to find them:.

I was also impressed with just the feel of walking the Mediterranean-vibed spaces between the buildings, even at this early stage when everything is still under construction.

Due to the hot desert climate of the region, everything is built around providing shade, breeze, and reflecting heat during the summer, while also maximizing the joyful fact that there is no winter there (the coldest month of the year still has an average daily high of 65F/18C, which means palm trees, leafy gardens and fruits and flowers forever.).

Recent findings suggest that with a setup like this, and 999 new neighbors to meet, I would rarely feel the need to leave the place. Which really cuts down on my desire to use a car. But on top of that, Culdesac has strategically placed itself in Tempe, a city right in the center of the Phoenix metro area, within walking distance of the main university and right on a light rail stop which allows you to reach almost everything (including the airport) for FREE, since an annual pass to the transit system is included with your rent.

But of course, you can also get around on foot, bike, e-bike, scooter, or hop into one of Culdesac’s fleet of rideshare electric cars for a trip to the mountains or whatever else you might want to do that’s outside of bike and transit range.

In a recent development, it’s insane. In fact it’s so good that I am going to attempt to move there myself at the end of 2023, enjoying my first escape from Colorado winter and celebrating the fact that my boy will be a legal adult at that time.

But even this is just a pilot project because Culdesac has much bigger plans.

From my conversations with the founders, I think they want to do this:.

So How Can We Benefit From This, and Support it?

And Then What Will Be Our Payback?

This whole change is exciting, and it is immense.

Understanding these ideas around city planning is the economic and social equivalent to being a doctor, and finding a 35-year-old patient in a hospital who is suffering from every chronic disease, but then discovering that they have been following a diet of Coke and Donuts for their whole lives and never been out on a walk, once.

In other words, the changes are so obvious, and the amount of win/win synergy so great, that every step we take towards making our cities better, and every car trip we eliminate, will absolutely explode our personal and national wealth upwards for generations to come.

The stakes just couldn’t be higher.

Another collaborator in the overall effort for car free cities is a bank-founding multi entrepreneur local friend named Kevin Dahlstrom. His recent Twitter rant on building car-free cities from the scratch gathered a shocking amount of very positive feedback and interesting comments.

* Despite my positive raving about this neighborhood, I have no financial or business connection with the project or any of the team members. I am just really excited about their work and want them to succeed!

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, I’ve spent close to the last decade as a personal trainer, and there is one piece of equipment I have come to prioritize in my home gym—no matter the season.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Industry observers note that if a cyclist is able to work strength training into their fitness routine, especially throughout the off-season, then the ceiling for potential power and speed goes up. The challenge is, as cyclists we just want to ride our bikes—driving to a gym, spending an hour or more in the weight room, then driving home is that much less time we’ll get in the saddle.

According to recent reports, I’ve spent close to the last decade as a personal trainer, and there is one piece of equipment I have come to prioritize in my home gym—no matter the season. The TRX Suspension Strap System is a versatile, compact, and burlier-than-expected piece of gym equipment. I’ve had the same pair since I was certified almost 10 years ago and they are still in great shape—even after loads of personal use as well as using them for in-home training sessions with clients.

One of the major reasons I continue to use the TRX system in my own workouts is because I can do a full-body strength workout, in a fraction of the time it takes me in the weight room, and I can do it all with one piece of equipment at home. All the TRX system needs is a way to mount it and enough room to do the exercises on the list.

Here, we’ll dig deeper into what TRX Suspension Straps are, why I recommend them to cyclists specifically, and give you a workout to jumpstart your season.

Industry observers note that TRX Suspension Straps are a suspension-based training tool designed to be used for bodyweight exercises. They were initially created by Randy Hetrick, a former U.S. Navy SEAL. He wanted to create a piece of fitness equipment that could offer full-body training and fit into a backpack—several iterations later, TRX was born. TRX Suspension Straps are basically a set of adjustable nylon straps that have handles to grab and cradles for feet. Most of the exercises you start with will have both hands on the handles, but as you progress you will start to add exercises with your feet in the cradles instead. The unique thing about this piece of equipment is that it can equally push a high-level athlete as well as offer things like balance improvement exercises. TRX bands can take simple exercises like a plank or a squat and offer modifications to make the exercise easier or create challenging progressions to make the exercise (much) harder. That makes them valuable for cyclists just starting out on a strength-training program or for those of us who have been doing it for years. The other great thing is they pack down really well. I have personally put them in the bottom of a carry-on bag on many trips over the years. You can set them up on everything from a traditional wall anchor to tree limbs and doorjambs. During my in-home personal training days, I had even set them up poolside for a great outdoor session with a client.

Sources indicate that cyclists benefit from some level of strength training off the bike. It’s one of the best ways to build speed, power, and durability. (Our Strength Training for Cyclists program, which is free to members, is packed with training prepares, strategies, and expert advice, making it a great place to get started or to elevate your current workouts.) With the TRX system, you can get all the benefits of strength training in with a tool that’s super effective. I like it because you can use it for moves that work your whole body, like an atomic push-up, which is when you perform a pushup with your feet in the bands, or something that isolates a muscle group, like a calf raise. Building a strong and sound core is a key to developing stability through the body.

One great thing about the TRX straps is that almost every exercise you do will help improve core stability. Increasing that stability will allow for better energy transfer through your body as you ride. The straps also are incredible for mobility and stretching, allowing you to get deeper into and out of stretches. They do this by allowing you an extra point of stability when your hands are holding the handles or cradles at the end of the straps.

Industry observers note that if you are setting these up in your home gym, you will need a way to mount the straps. They come with a carabiner attached to the straps, but that has to get clipped to something. I typically use a double-length nylon sling used for climbing because I had a few of these lying around that I retired from my climbing rack. TRX also makes specific straps, wall anchors, and even doorjamb anchors to set the straps up on just about anything you can think of. Pro tip—make sure the anchor you use for the straps is strong enough to hold more than bodyweight.

I have been using my own set of the TRX Straps for over a decade now and they show few signs of wear. During my time as a personal trainer, I used the suspension straps for everyone from elite athletes to people in their seventies and eighties just looking to improve balance and mobility. They can handle everything from explosive training days to core and stability training. For cyclists that are looking to build a stronger core, here are a few of my favorite exercises.

In a recent development, you can find our complete expert-recommended workout here. The exercises, demonstrated by Susane Pata, TRX senior master instructor, will build the strength, stability, and mobility cyclists need. You can do the warmup moves anytime you want to wake up your muscles before a ride, and the stretches to loosen up when you’re done.

A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

The Anti-Movement Core Routine Every Runner Needs

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (795 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Triathlete

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • (Photo: Aleksandr Kondratov, Getty).
  • Sources indicate that for this article, physical therapist Jennie Hansen analyzed a latest study on anti-movement vs.
  • In a recent development, “Core strengthening” is a term runners frequently toss around.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Glute bridge post-run. (Photo: Aleksandr Kondratov, Getty).

Sources indicate that for this article, physical therapist Jennie Hansen analyzed a latest study on anti-movement vs. dynamic core training and built a simple, science-backed core routine for runners based on the findings. The routine targets the deep stabilizing muscles that protect your spine and improve performance.

In a recent development, “Core strengthening” is a term runners frequently toss around. We all know we need it. But what exactly is it, and what should it entail? (Hint: Not crunches.).

Recent findings suggest that when we talk about the core, we mean the abdominal muscles, low back, gluteal, pelvic, and hip muscles that support the spine and trunk. These muscles include both smaller, deep groups that attach directly to the spine to provide stabilization and larger, more global ones that can assist with stability and produce movement.

Why do we need this area to be strong? Well, even non-runners need to pay attention to their core strength to avoid lower back pain, which is the top cause of years lived with disability. Athletically, the core must create proximal stability to allow for powerful, efficient movements distally—which requires adequate strength combined with coordinated neuromuscular activation and control. So, core strength is certainly vital for pain reduction, injury prevention, and athletic performance.

Sources indicate that when running, the trunk serves to provide a stable base of support so that the legs can effectively generate the forces that create forward movement. These forces are transferred across the trunk and counterbalanced by the arms, requiring coordination between the hips, trunk muscles, and shoulders.

In a recent development, while running appears to be purely a forward (sagittal plane) activity, the trunk muscles are hard at work controlling side-to-side (frontal plane) and rotational (transverse plane) forces. Muscle activation and timing change with speed, with higher speeds generally requiring more control and work. The deep trunk muscles also contribute to respiration.

While some small trunk motion naturally occurs with running, excessive motion is detrimental. Increased trunk flexion is associated with decreased running economy and increased loading rates and vertical impact forces. Increased lateral trunk lean has also been linked to increased loading rates, which may play a role in the development of certain injuries.

Even though most of us know that crunches are out, there’s still plenty of confusion about how to train our cores. While strength work doesn’t need to look exactly like running, it does need to meet (and exceed) its demands—meaning that stability should be emphasized over motion.

In a recent development, enter a recent study comparing neuromuscular activation between “anti-movement” and “dynamic” core training. Unlike traditional dynamic core exercises, which work the trunk and spinal musculature by moving through flexion, extension, rotation, and side bending, anti-movement exercises resist external forces, forcing stabilization throughout the trunk—basically, trunk isometrics.

The 12-week study compared a combination of Pallof holds and plank variations (incorporating bands and the TRX suspension trainer for progression) in the anti-movement program against a dynamic program that included exercises such as sit-ups, leg raises, jack knives, Russian twists, windshield wipers, and back extensions (incorporating Swiss balls for progression).

While both exercise groups demonstrated enhancements in neuromuscular efficiency compared to a control group, improvements were overall greater in the anti-movement group, particularly within the deep local musculature that activates prior to limb movement and plays an important role in stabilizing the spine.

The authors therefore hypothesized that this enhanced neuromuscular efficiency could improve endurance, delay fatigue, and reduce the need for recruitment of larger, more global muscles—thus protecting the spine and potentially decreasing injury risk while improving performance.

In a recent development, runners can apply these findings and consider an “anti-movement”-focused core routine, similar to the one used in the study. Nothing fancy or extensive is required—just one exercise each to resist the trunk’s motions (flexion, extension, rotation, and side-bending/lateral flexion). Simple plank variations and other holds work well to streamline your core routine efficiently and effectively.

Targets: Anti-extension · full core (local and global).

The front plank is a classic core stability exercise that falls into the anti-extension category, challenging most of both the local and global core muscles.

Targets: Anti-flexion · spinal extensors and glutes.

While the study used a supine plank as its anti-flexion exercise, the shoulder position required could be a limiter, so bridge holds are likely a more practical way for many runners to work the posterior trunk muscles, including the spinal extensors and gluteals.

Targets: Anti-lateral flexion · lateral trunk and hip muscles.

The side plank can be considered an anti-lateral-flexion exercise, challenging the lateral trunk and hip musculature.

Targets: Anti-rotation · obliques and deep abdominal rotators.

The Pallof press is a common anti-rotation exercise, challenging the deep abdominal rotators, including the obliques.

Tech Report: Is Your Body Fat Percentage Holding Back Your Cycling Goals? The Answer Depends on Your Age and Ambition.

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (895 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, for cyclists, body composition is a critical performance factor that goes beyond aesthetics.
  • Understanding age and typical body fat percentage ranges gives us valuable context for setting realistic and healthy body composition goals and determining whether our focus should be on fat loss, strength building, or overall health.
  • 🚴🏻‍♀️ Ready to unlock a stronger, healthier you?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, for cyclists, body composition is a critical performance factor that goes beyond aesthetics. It directly influences climbing speed, power endurance, and recovery capabilities. Average body-fat percentage averages and recommendations shift as we age depending on individual goals, and whether we’re a recreational rider or a competitive cyclist pursuing maximum power-to-weight ratio.

Understanding age and typical body fat percentage ranges gives us valuable context for setting realistic and healthy body composition goals and determining whether our focus should be on fat loss, strength building, or overall health. (It’s notable to note that body fat percentage and BMI (body mass index) are not the same thing.).

🚴🏻‍♀️ Ready to unlock a stronger, healthier you? Our Cycling for Weight Loss program will help you find confidence and consistency in your training.

Recent findings suggest that there isn’t a universally “right” body-fat percentage. Ideal targets depend on sex, age, activity level, and specific goals, in addition to whether you’re prioritizing general health, recreational fitness, or competitive performance. However, there are commonly used target ranges per decade that coaches, trainers, and sports scientists use as healthy guidelines (which should be treated as approximate).

Recent findings suggest that let’s examine “average” body fat percentages guidelines by decade, what the average body fat percentages are for men and women in the United States, and the impact of different measurement methods (DEXA scan, home body fat scale, InBody scan) on results. These averages should be regarded as benchmarks for setting achievable, performance-oriented goals, not as rigid targets. They serve as a navigational tool rather than a mandatory destination.

20s: Competitive athletes: 6–10 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 11–15 percent, Healthy range: 12–20 percent.

30s: Competitive athletes: 7–11 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 12–16 percent, Healthy range: 14–22 percent.

40s: Competitive athletes: 8–12 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 13–17 percent, Healthy range: 16–24 percent.

50s: Competitive athletes: 9–13 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 14–18 percent, Healthy range: 18–26 percent.

60+: Competitive athletes: 10–14 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 15–19 percent, Healthy range: 20–28 percent.

20s: Competitive athletes: 14–18 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 19–23 percent, Healthy range: 20–30 percent.

30s: Competitive athletes: 15–19 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 20–24 percent, Healthy range: 22–32 percent.

40s: Competitive athletes: 16–20 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 21–25 percent, 50s: Competitive athletes: 17–21 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 22–26 percent, Healthy range: 26–36 percent.

60+: Competitive athletes: 18–22 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 23–27 percent, Healthy range: 28–38 percent.

Cyclists specializing in climbing typically aim for the lower end of these ranges, though excessively rapid fat loss can compromise strength and power.

Industry observers note that while the ranges above are recommended guidelines, the actual averages for folks according to the CDC look pretty different. The following data on average body fat percentage of men and women in the U. S. has been collected through the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey.

According to recent reports, it’s important to note that the body fat percentage measurement method really matters. Home scales that measure body fat percentage can be quite inaccurate according to researchers. In my own experience, an InBody scan (which is the measurement method I recommend for a more reliable assessment, by the way) revealed that my body fat percentage is several percentage points higher than what the home body fat scale I have been testing had measured.

According to recent reports, however, even InBody results can fluctuate with hydration levels. DEXA scans offer the most stable results but are generally more expensive. The key is to track trends over time rather than focusing on single numbers.

When it comes to fat loss, aim for a safe and healthy pace of 0.5-1 percent of body weight per week, while prioritizing preserving lean mass through optimal protein intake and strength training. However, it can be tricky to determine how much of the body weight lost is fat, and factors like how lean someone already is, a person’s metabolism, and training intensity also play a role.

It has been revealed that as an example, in one study of female volunteers on reduced-calorie diets, participants were assigned exercise programs of varying intensity. According to the researchers, the women doing a moderate exercise program lost 6.2 percent body fat over three months on average, which added up to being about 2 percent a month. The intense exercise group lost an average of approximately 10 percent body fat over the same time period, which comes out to around 3.3 percent per month.

In a recent development, understanding body composition is a valuable tool for cyclists looking to optimize their performance and achieve their goals. By considering your age, sex, activity level, and using reliable measurement methods, you can set realistic targets and tailor your training and nutrition strategies accordingly. Remember, it's all about finding the right balance for your body and your goals.

In a recent development, natascha Grief is the fitness and reviews editor for Women’s Health. She writes about fitness, health, performance, everyday movement, and the products that help people train and recover better. She brings more than a decade of experience as a NASM-certified personal trainer focused on training women, with specialties in functional strength training, corrective exercise, nutrition, and behavior change. She previously worked as the health and fitness editor at Bicycling, and her writing has appeared in Runner’s World and other outlets. Across her work, she’s especially focused on making complex wellness, training, and performance topics approachable and accessible.

Recent findings suggest that fall riding season is coming to a close, and winter is right around the corner. While late fall and winter mean shorter daylight hours for riding, it’s a great time to save on cycling gear—for yourself or if shopping early for holiday gifts. Many brands are discounting old inventory at great prices, and others are clearing room for newly introduced gear hitting shelves after the New Year.

According to recent reports, although many of the best holiday sales aren’t until Black Friday and Cyber Monday, some retailers are running Early Black Friday promotions with significant deals and discounts on top-rated gear. In addition to Pre-Black Friday sales, Amazon, REI, bike brands, and other retailers are offering deep discounts on cycling equipment, components, apparel, and accessories you need for road, gravel, and mountain bike rides.

Sources indicate that pre-Black Friday sales are a great chance to stock up on frequently used consumables—such as tubes, tire sealant, chain lube, and nutrition products—and to grab the gear you need for late-fall and winter rides. They’re also a great way to save money on usually pricey riding apparel: If you’ve been holding out on buying a new vest, arm warmers, jerseys, a jacket, or even shoes, some brands are offering deep discounts on cycling clothing and accessories.

Below are sales and deals hubs for several top online cycling gear and bike retailers, plus links to sales from leading clothing brands and bike companies. These are some of the best deals on editor-tested gear we’ve spotted so far. Bookmark this page and return for updates as even more deals come online.

Bike lights are a must-have item for anyone commuting or riding road or gravel in the winter months. Even if you already have a light, I’ve found it super useful to own an extra set to have at the office, on my other bikes, or as spares for friends.

According to recent reports, lezyne consistently makes great front and rear lights. While slightly pricier than budget picks found on Amazon or AliExpress, they’re durable, work well, and last several seasons. Plus, we’ve found Lezyne’s advertised runtimes and lumens are much closer to reality than many no-name lights.

Showers Pass makes our best-tested winter gloves, and they’re currently on sale at 19% off. In their review, our test rider noted, “This knit, waterproof glove has a midweight feel and sufficient insulation when temperatures hover around freezing. Most riders will find the Crosspoints reach its limit at about 30-35 degrees, depending on how hard you’re riding.”.

The glove traps some body heat, so your fingers may be slightly chilly at first but will warm up within 15 minutes. Better yet, when the mercury climbs, your hands won’t feel hot and sweaty.

Recent findings suggest that electric mini-inflators burst onto the scene a couple of years ago and have rapidly become a rider favorite for pumping up your tires at home, at the trailhead, or on rides. Of the inflators we’ve tested, the RockBros model stands out for its consistency and is a favorite of Bicycling editors. It’s compact, lightweight, and has an accurate gauge. In our testing of 15 electric pumps, it inflated a road tire to 65 psi in 45 seconds, and filled five tires before running out of power.

The Wahoo Kickr Core 2—Bicycling’s Best Overall Indoor Trainer—is on sale for the lowest price we’ve seen: $399.99. The Core combines excellent performance, great accuracy, and high max resistance in a package perfect for Zwift rides after work, winter training, and even competitive virtual racing.

It has been revealed that indoor training bikes are quickly gaining popularity for their ease of use and low maintenance. With a dedicated indoor setup, you no longer have to wrestle with getting your bike on or off the smart trainer, which also makes it convenient to share with other riders in your family. Plus, you won’t wear out pricey parts. Zwift’s Ride is our favorite: it sets up quickly and adjusts for a wide range of rider heights and fits. It also costs thousands less than its competitors.

Shorter daylight hours and lower temps often mean fewer hours spent riding outside on the road or trail. An indoor trainer helps you maintain your fitness through the winter months while getting your riding fix. Garmin’s Tacx Flux2 is the brand’s mid-range smart trainer; with 2,000 watts of resistance, it simulates gradients up to 16%. The Flux also connects to virtual platforms like Zwift and Rouvy for immersive indoor riding experiences.

According to recent reports, stainless bottles have become popular among cyclists over the past several seasons. They keep water chilled on hot rides and don’t give your water a funny plastic taste. Many gravel and off-road riders love CamelBak’s Stainless Podium, particularly for its open/closed twist-lock cap. The Podium Stainless also ranked best in our heat testing last summer and performed well in our winter bottle testing.

SUMMER BOTTLE TESTING WINTER BOTTLE TESTING.

Sources indicate that elite road and gravel helmets offer low weight, excellent ventilation, and great looks. However, those benefits usually come at a high cost. Giro’s Agilis Mips helmet is a great option if you want a pro-level look and performance without the associated price.

Sources indicate that weighing 299 grams (size medium), my Agilis is only 15 grams heavier than Giro’s premium Aries Spherical model—and the Agilis costs significantly less. The Agilis is very well-ventilated, comparable to the priciest lids on all but the hottest of rides.

This helmet features Mips technology to protect your brain from rotational forces in a crash, and Giro’s Hardbody co-molded shell to better protect it from small bumps and dings when not on your head. Plus, the Agilis uses the Roc-Loc dial system to ensure a proper fit.

Recent findings suggest that MET’s Trenta 3K Carbon is one of the top five road helmets by Virginia Tech’s helmet lab. It’s also one of the best for racing and high-performance riding, as proven by UAE Team Emirates’s results—Tour de France champion Tadej Pogačar and World Champion Brandon McNulty. While UAE riders often race the Italian brand’s Manta aero helmet, they pick the lightweight, well-ventilated Trenta 3K Carbon for climbing stages and training.

It has been revealed that unlike some modern helmets with similarly strong protection, the Trenta feels light and racey on your head, and almost disappears when you’re riding. The straps offer good adjustability, and the Mips Air Node liner protects without feeling bulky. However, the Trenta’s biggest drawback is its price tag. Typically priced over $500, this is an expensive piece of kit, but this deal cuts the cost by almost a third.

Arm warmers are among the most versatile pieces of cycling clothing you can own. This magical piece of kit turns your short-sleeve jersey into a long-sleeve in seconds—and you can change back to short sleeves again mid-ride if the temps rise.

It has been revealed that I’ve owned many pairs of arm warmers over the last three decades, and I rarely ride without them on my arms or in my jersey pocket if the temperatures are between 45 and 60 degrees. Castelli makes some of the best clothes out there, and these arm warmers are a steal for the price. They’re easy to pull on or off while riding, and they don’t sag.

A quality rain jacket is a must-have item for riders who live anywhere it rains or snows. Rapha’s Core Rain Jacket is great option for layering over your winter jersey without adding too much bulk. It features a two-way zip for regulating body temperature, reflective hits for riding after dusk or in the early morning, and packs down small if weather clears mid-ride.

If you ride in temps below 40 degrees, a good cycling jacket is a great asset. As a Scottish brand, Endura knows a few things about riding in the cold, dark days of winter, and its MT500 Freezing Point jacket is a great option for trail rides and commuting in low temps. It features PrimaLoft Gold insulation and a DWR finish to shed rain drops. Another great feature is the MT500’s underarm zippers; they allow you to cool off and ventilate without unzipping your entire jacket.

When cold weather hits, bib tights ensure you stay warm on rides. Of the many cycling tights available, Velocio makes some of our test editors’ favorites. The One Thermal bibs feature a soft, fleece lining and use a more relaxed, less compressive fit than some of the brands’ other options. This makes them perfect for road, gravel, and trail rides, or even layering under commuter pants.

Instead of shredding your nice, lightweight road tires on weather-worn winter roads, swap them out for more durable rubber. Vittoria’s Rubino tires are a proven all-season road tire with a smooth, fast-rolling center and siped edges for cornering traction. They’re tubeless-compatible, so you’ll catch fewer flats in the cold, and come in widths from 26mm to 34mm with black or tan sidewalls.

Modern bike computers do much more than display speed and distance. These devices are a critical information hub for many cyclists. Cycling computers can record ride metrics, display real-time performance data, and help you navigate—but that’s only scratching the surface of their capabilities.

According to recent reports, the Elemnt Bolt 3 is Wahoo’s tiny-but-mighty cycling-specific computer. Wahoo equips it with a 2.3-inch high-resolution screen, up to 20 hours of battery life, and integration with Strava, Komoot, and other popular cycling platforms.

Another great option is the Hammerhead Karoo. This head unit features a 3.2-inch color touchscreen Gorilla Glass display and up to 35 hours of run time. The Karoo stands out for its mapping and navigation. The navigation, combined with its pop-up hill climb feature and ability to sideload apps, makes the Karoo my overall favorite.

It has been revealed that POC makes comfortable, well-ventilated helmets for road, gravel, and mountain biking. The Kortal is a trail-style helmet, featuring an adjustable visor, room to stow your glasses or goggles, and plenty of airflow for hot summer trail rides. The straps are also comfortable, something that often bugs me on other lids.

Recent findings suggest that fresh bar tape is the quickest and most cost-effective way to improve the look, feel, and comfort of any road or gravel bike. I’ve used Fizik tape on several bikes that have come in for testing, and have also bought it for my personal bikes. It has enough cushion, reliable grip, and is easy to wrap. You can’t ask for much more from bar tape.

While many riders are adding electric mini-inflators to their tool kits, a quality floor pump remains an essential part of every cyclist’s arsenal. They never run out of batteries, pump as many tires as your arms can handle, and are easy to use.

Industry observers note that riders and mechanics have trusted Topeak’s JoeBlow pumps for decades—because they work. Although many JoeBlow models are low-cost and utilitarian, the JoeBlow Ace DX is a Cadillac-level floor pump. It features alloy construction with a metal chuck and can inflate tires up to 260 psi, with three different inflation modes: high-volume, standard, or high-pressure.

The stability counterpart to the Ghost 18, the Adrenaline GTS is the shoe many of us ran in when we fell in love with running. The 25th iteration is the lightest yet, with a foamy midsole, the brand’s DNA Loft v3, to absorb shock and provide soft landings. The guide rails system is Brooks’s unobtrusive stability tech for neutral runners and overpronators alike. Dense foam on the medial and lateral sides acts as bumpers to help align your knee and ankle.

“This is a fantastic shoe,” said tester Chris Garges, an overpronator and heel striker. “I’ve run in every model Adrenaline dating back to the Adrenaline 3, and this is by far the best shoe in the series. I loved everything from the fit to the ride to the cushioning.”.

Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 Review.

Industry observers note that brooks wanted to change what we should expect when running in a max-cushioned trainer. “We noticed that for some people, they would start running in a neutral shoe and then their body would work extra. So the internal cost was actually increasing,” stated Brooks Footwear PLM and BlueLine Director Nikhil Jain.

Recent findings suggest that the team set out to create a shoe that would cut that internal cost. The Glycerin Flex has a decoupled heel and Flex Zone; these components allow your foot to flex naturally instead of working against a stiff, beefy platform.

Industry observers note that “Testing the Brooks Glycerin Flex was a novel experience for me on multiple fronts,” said Editorial Assistant Michael McDonough. “Not only was this the first Brooks running shoe I’ve ever run in, but it was also the first hyperflexible shoe that I have ever seen—and overall, it was a positive experience. The Glycerin Flex combines the benefits of a daily trainer that allows your feet to work and get stronger with the comfort and protection of a maximalist shoe.”.

We like the Glycerin Max 2 for run/walking and recovery days. The shoe has 45 mm of DNA Tuned foam in the heel and a 6 mm offset. Its beefiness was off-putting for some, especially for runners hoping to get in some tempo work on their long runs. But testers said the cushioning was extremely comfy on slow days.

“I loved how comfortable the sneaker was. I instantly felt supported and it felt like I was walking on a bouncy pillow,” said wear-tester Steph Norman. “This sneaker would be great for easy/long miles where you do not have to worry about your feet hurting.”.

In a recent development, the popular Brooks Ghost hits the trails. The shoe is outfitted for going off-road with 3 mm lugs on the TrailTack rubber outsole.

In a recent development, our tester, David Hinkl, appreciated how the shoe protected his feet on gnarly surfaces. “The best part of the shoe for me was the sole,” he noted. “It was beefy enough to prevent sharp rocks and pointy things from getting to my feet. Training is more fun when I don’t have to tiptoe across the trail.”.

Recent findings suggest that the Canopy is iconic. Despite the curtains of rain, monstrous winds, and cold temps, Des Linden was the first American woman to win the 2018 Boston Marathon after 33 years. And she wore the Canopy Jacket. This version of the Canopy (the original is also on sale with 30 percent off) can be packed into a little pouch that’s easy to store in the depths of an overpacked duffel.

In a recent development, the High Point keeps out the rain without overheating. Venting in the back allows airflow, while waterproof fabric and sealed inner seams keep you from getting soaked during a downpour. The jacket also packs down into a pocket.

These joggers are the softest joggers we’ve tested. They’re great for warmups, cooldowns, and traveling. I should know—I trekked Japan after running the Tokyo Marathon in these.

The Run Visible not only ensures you’re seen with reflective detail, but it also keeps you warm thanks to Thermolite insulation. Three pockets provide storage. That hi-vis orange color also helps you pop out in low light.

The Chaser is for runners who love a soft compression short with ample storage. The high-rise Chaser has side pockets for stashing your phone and leg-opening grippers to prevent them from riding up.

Garmin LiveTrack Now Alerts Waze Drivers to Nearby Cyclists

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (678 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Rearview radars are one of our favorite cycling accessories because they alert riders when a vehicle is approaching from behind.
  • It has been revealed that here’s how it works.
  • Waze states the alert comes when a cyclist gets closer, but it hasn’t specified the distance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rearview radars are one of our favorite cycling accessories because they alert riders when a vehicle is approaching from behind. Now Garmin and Waze are flipping that warning around: Their new partnership alerts drivers when a cyclist using Garmin’s LiveTrack is nearby.

It has been revealed that here’s how it works. Start an outdoor cycling activity with LiveTrack on a compatible Garmin Edge computer or smartwatch, and your location will appear in Waze as a moving cyclist icon. Drivers don’t need to be navigating a route to see cyclists; Waze told me the icons appear whenever the app is open, as riders enter the driver’s broader route area or immediate surroundings.

Waze states the alert comes when a cyclist gets closer, but it hasn’t specified the distance. In an email response to my questions, Garmin told me alerts go to “relevant drivers,” usually when the rider and driver are on the same road and traveling in the same direction. A cyclist farther ahead on the driver’s mapped route may also trigger one.

In a recent development, if several riders are together, Waze reveals one icon to avoid repeat alerts. If they spread out, multiple icons appear. Garmin describes the grouping feature as “built-in clustering logic.”.

Recent findings suggest that for Waze users, cyclist alerts are on by default but can be turned off in the app’s settings. Riders opt in to Waze sharing through Garmin, but only once. After that, sharing starts whenever they begin a cycling LiveTrack, whether they start it manually or set it to start automatically.

Garmin says any Edge computer or smartwatch with LiveTrack is compatible. LiveTrack requires a phone paired with Garmin Connect and cellular coverage; Garmin’s LTE-enabled devices can run LiveTrack without relying on the phone’s connection.

No additional subscription or purchase is required. Waze indicates drivers see only a temporary alert that a cyclist is nearby, not the rider’s name, identity, or exact route. Sharing stops when the ride ends.

This is not V2X, the connected-vehicle technology that has been simmering in the background. V2X systems let vehicles exchange information with one another, roadside infrastructure, and other road users, including cyclists. Garmin and Waze are taking an app-based route to a similar goal: LiveTrack sends a rider’s location to Waze, which can alert drivers using the app.

It’s a sensible idea, but it requires the latest apps and firmware, a Garmin rider who has opted in, a working connection, and a driver using Waze. It isn’t a substitute for cycling-friendly infrastructure, and it won’t fix distracted drivers or jerks in cars. But reminding drivers that cyclists are on the road is a step in the right direction.

It has been revealed that would you enable Waze sharing for your LiveTrack rides? If you use Waze while driving, would a cyclist icon or alert change how you approach the road? Tell us in the comments, or join me on Discord. I’d especially like to hear from riders who already use LiveTrack or Waze: What would you want to know before turning this on?

I would genuinely use this for any type of run: easy miles, tempo, speed work, hard intervals, long runs, etc. I love putting it on for an easy run and letting the legs just feel more pop and quick turnover than I normally feel on an easy mileage day.”.

Industry observers note that we love the Guide 18 because it’s a stability shoe that’s just so darn comfy. Don’t believe me? Then read it straight from tester Dave Block’s shoe feedback form:.

Industry observers note that “The first time I tried on the shoe, I cracked a big smile. I *loved* the feel. It’s just so darn soft and comfortable inside! It put me in a positive frame of mind before I went out the door. If memory serves, this shoe has the most comfortable interior of all the ones I’ve wear-tested.

The shoe features Saucony’s Center Path technology, which uses asymmetric midsole geometry and a wider midfoot. This translates to unobtrusive support for overpronators and late-onset overpronators alike.

In a recent development, the Ghost Max is a plusher version of your favorite daily trainer. The shoe is a terrific walker or mattress-soft shoe for the injury-prone. Its accommodating fit creates a roomy footbed for orthotics wearers, and the DNA Loft v3 foam delivers ultimate shock absorption for sore knees and long efforts.

Sources indicate that “The Brooks Ghost Max 3 serves great as an everyday trainer for beginner to intermediate runners who prioritize comfort first and are looking to log many casual miles,” said tester James Prekopa. “The relatively light and lean ride makes it easy to enter a flow state. I found this shoe to be ideal for solid surfaces like pavement and concrete. These surfaces let you maximize the shoe's comfort features without feeling like you’re sinking too much. This shoe is for someone who prioritizes comfort first, stability second, and performance last.”.

According to recent reports, when your legs have given up, and so has your brain, this is the shoe you grab for. It’s made for long run comfort, durability, and versatility. It’s a max-cushioned trainer that is typically well-priced, but right now, that price is basically unbeatable.

Industry observers note that wear tester Nick Miller is a massive fan. He loved how his efforts didn’t leave him aching and sore. He mentioned that “Everything from the foam on the bottom of the shoe to the padding around the collar was very ‘cushy’ and comfortable. #103205. Triathlon as the Newly introduced Run Club: Community Without “Bro Culture”

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2974 w)
